#780. Tom Brady in talks over buying Chelsea stake after Birmingham City exit

NFL legend was Chelsea guest at Club World Cup

Brady has good relationship with Behdad Eghbali

Tom Brady is in discussions about buying a small stake in Chelsea. The NFL legend sold a minority share in Birmingham City this month after three years, a move sources said was to pave the way for investing at Stamford Bridge.

Brady was a guest of Chelsea when they won the Club World Cup in New Jersey last year and was seen celebrating with the players after their remarkable 3-0 final win over Paris Saint-Germain.

The seven-time Super Bowl winner is understood to have a good relationship with Behdad Eghbali, whose fund, Clearlake Capital, owns 86.5% of Chelsea after Todd Boehly and Mark Walter sold their shares in September.

Brady bought into Birmingham in August 2023, less than a year after his second and final retirement from the NFL, after the club’s takeover by Tom Wagner’s Knighthead Capital.

Brady was appointed chair of the club’s advisory board and had a prominent role in the 2025 Amazon Prime documentary Built in Birmingham: Brady & The Blues, which made headlines when he questioned the “work ethic” of Wayne Rooney, who was the manager.

In announcing Brady’s departure the club said: “Birmingham City Football Club expresses its sincere gratitude to Tom Brady for his involvement with and unwavering support for the club over the last three years.”

Brady owns a minority stake in the NFL team Las Vegas Raiders, which he purchased alongside Wagner.

#779. How Grand Theft Auto 6 Already Raced It’s Way Into Red Carpet Fashion

With Grand Theft Auto VI already set to become the biggest game of 2026 after its Nov. 19 launch, model Alex Consani—who lent her voice to the game—showed off her GTA 6-inspired outfit.

Alex Consani is ready for a spin around Vice City.

With the supermodel lending her voice to Grand Theft Auto VI—which is poised to be the biggest video game of the year after making $3.79 billion in preorder and first-day sales, according to parent company Take Two—it was only appropriate that she channel that car vibe into her clutch look for the game’s launch party.

Consani buckled up for the Nov. 18 event at the Gekko restaurant in Miami wearing a short dress from Paris-based label Sevali’s spring 2025 collection that was made out of upcycled seatbelts. The belts crisscrossed around the 23-year-old’s svelte figure, coming to a click—literally—with a buckle that was strapped across her shoulder.

The Victoria’s Secret model completed her look with clear kitten heels and her long blonde hair parted down the middle and flowing behind her.

In the newly released video game, Consani can be heard as a DJ for the in-game radio station Flash FM alongside singer Robyn. The two play songs from the likes of Olivia Rodrigo, Charli XCX, Zara Larsson and more as they put their commentary into high gear.

After playing Rodrigo’s “good 4 u,” Consani can be heard saying in a clip posted from the game, “How do you even fumble a baddie like Olivia?”

She also had some love for Charli XCX, saying, “Whatever Charli XCX does, she’s my medicine. That is my f--king doctor, y’all.”

As for Larsson? After playing the Swedish singer’s hit “Fast Emotion,” Consani commented, “God, I love Zara so much.”

Of course, the model isn’t the only star to lend her voice to GTA VI, with Bad Bunny coming in as host of Latin radio Cocoteo FM, PinkPantheress DJing the indie dance station Stockyard FM, “Weird” Al Yankovic hosting the ’80s station Vice City FM, Morgan Wallen and Lana Del Rey co-hosting Back Country Radio and Rolling Stones guitarist Keith Richards playing his part as DJ Keith on Gloriana Blues Radio.

Grand Theft Auto VI marks the latest installment in the long-running video game series, coming out 13 years after the record-breaking Grand Theft Auto V.

The new game features characters like Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos as they take part in fan-favorite activities from previous games like car-jackings, shootouts, street-racing, robberies, swimming, jet-skiing, sky-diving, visiting the strip club and, yes, even petting dogs. GTA 6 is set around locations inspired by Floria, allowing players new playable vehicles like kayaks and airboats to roam around the new locale.

#778. Mathematician says he and AI solved Riemann hypothesis — the field’s biggest outstanding challenge

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The Riemann hypothesis has been a lodestar for generations of mathetmaticians. Credit: James Brittain/Getty

In a year that has seen artificial intelligence reach one spectacular mathematical breakthrough after another, Anthropic is now claiming the top prize of them all: a full proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the statement that many mathematicians consider the most important open problem in the field.

The announcement came from Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at the San Francisco, California company. “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote, referring to Anthropic’s large language model (LLM).

“If this fully checks out, it is clearly a historic milestone in mathematics,” says number theorist James Maynard, a Fields Medal winner at the University of Oxford, UK, says.

It would also be a spectacular bicentenary present for Bernhard Riemann, the German mathematician who was born 200 years ago this September and who formulated the problem, which addresses the distribution of prime numbers, in the mid-1800.

The problem has to do with the ‘Riemann ζ function’ (ζ is the Greek letter zeta), which encodes the randomness properties of the prime numbers. Riemann discovered that the distribution of primes is encoded in the ζ function’s ‘zeroes.’ These are points on a plane denoted by z satisfying the equation ζ(z) = 0.

Riemann conjectured that apart from some obvious but uninteresting cases, all such solutions had to lie on a certain vertical line in the plane. If this were true, he showed, it would imply that prime numbers are scattered among all whole numbers in a way that is essentially as random as it could be.

Alpöge’s 4-page document includes a sketch of the proof. But Andrew Granville, a number theorist at the University of Montreal in Canada, says that Alpöge should have taken the time to prepare a clearer write-up before making the announcement, which came just days after Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO). The IPO initially valued the company at US$1.5 trillion, but the company’s valuation dropped on 19 November.

“What he released is garbled,” Granville says of Alpöge’s document. Granville cites the downturn in the company’s stock value as the reason for the timing of the proof’s release.

“There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false,” Alpöge wrote in the document.

Anthropic did not respond immediately to Nature’s request for comment.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03812-7

#777. First defeat and first red for Ferguson as Glentoran falter

Ferguson was sent off in just his fourth game as Glentoran manager

It was a night of unfortunate firsts for Duncan Ferguson at Solitude on Friday.

The Everton great suffered his first defeat as Glentoran boss as they were edged out 3-2 by Cliftonville in an Irish Premiership thriller.

He also received his first red card as a manager, after picking up nine during his playing career, in the first half for protesting the decision to award Cliftonville's first goal after he perceived a foul in the build-up.

The defeat ended Glentoran's eight-game unbeaten run in the league and leaves them well off the pace in pursuit of their first league title since 2009.

While he has delivered with his animated touchline antics, Ferguson has so far struggled to get much out of his side on the pitch.

Ferguson sent off as Reds beat Glens in thriller - report and highlights

The Glens were second best for much of the first half in north Belfast, with Cliftonville dominating possession and creating the better chances.

Still, the awarding of the Reds' first goal was controversial as it looked like defender Jarlath O'Rourke had been pushed by Liam McStravick, who then teed up Joe Sheridan to score the opener on 38 minutes.

Ferguson was incensed that the goal stood, protesting while his side went up the other end and scored an equaliser through Cal Weatherup's deflected strike a minute later.

Such was the vehemence of his words towards the officials, referee Ben McMaster brandished a straight red card and Ferguson was forced to make the long walk to the tunnel all while being jeered by Cliftonville supporters.

"I think the manager got frustrated because it was a foul. It changes the dynamic [the sending off], he's a leader, I've then got to step in and fill his boots and it's a big set of boots to fill," said Ferguson's assistant Gary Bollan.

His side looked to have received a stern talking to from Bollan at half-time as they were much more competitive after the break.

They responded to Brian Healy putting the Reds ahead once again with a fine James Douglas strike on 86 minutes, which looked to be enough to secure a point and continue their unbeaten run.

However, they failed to stop midfielder Sheridan, who waltzed into the box before firing into the top corner two minutes later to seal a win.

Glentoran's fifth league defeat of the campaign leaves them 14 points behind pacesetters Linfield.

Former Crusaders captain Colin Coates, who was on co-commentary duties for the game for BBC Sport NI, believes Ferguson and the club have "a lot of work to do" to get back challenging for major honours.

"Look at the squad, there is work to do in January and next summer," he added.

"Duncan Ferguson will use this next few months to assess what he has, what he wants to keep and what he needs to bring in to make them competitive. Every time I watch them I want more from them.

"There is a real lack of quality particularly at the top end they don't look like they can hurt teams aside from Jordan Stewart. A lot of work and soul searching to do and players will be playing for their futures."

Stewart was suspended for the game at Solitude and was a big miss while Ferguson will hope to get more out of Conor McMenamin and the fit-again Pat Hoban, who both came on in the second half.

The Glens face two games against Larne, one in the BetMcLean Cup on Tuesday and one in the league next Friday and Ferguson will hope to mastermind two big results to really kick-start his reign.

Sheridan scored two fine goals in Cliftonville's victory

For Cliftonville, it was a case of another big performance under the lights on a Friday in front of a raucous Solitude crowd.

The Reds beat Larne 4-2 at the same venue a fortnight ago and key in their two big wins in recent weeks has been teenage midfielder Sheridan, who is growing in stature for Jim Magilton.

The 19-year-old broke into the senior squad last season after a fruitful six-month spell at Queen's University in the 2024-25 campaign.

He won the club's Young Player of the Year award last season and was a rotation option, but he has kicked on again this year and firmly established himself in a midfield three with captain Rory Hale and Dean McMaster.

The next step for the talented Northern Ireland under-21 international is adding goals and assists to his game and he certainly delivered on Friday.

Former Glentoran captain Paul Leeman said he showed "composure" for both his goals, first to curl home from close range, then to weave his way into the box and place the ball in the top corner.

"It was a really good performance from him. He's becoming a mainstay in the team," Leeman added.

The victory moves Cliftonville to within a point of the Glens and with games against struggling Ballymena United and Bangor to come, they will hope to embark upon another winning run to continue their surge up the table.

#776. Chelsea fined £150,000 for discriminatory chanting

Chelsea have been fined Â£150,000 by the Football Association as part of a punishment for anti-Catholic and anti-Irish chants during an FA Cup third-round win at Charlton Athletic in January.

The club have also been warned about their future conduct and had an action plan imposed on them in relation to the offence.

"Chelsea FC failed to ensure its spectators and/or supporters (and anyone purporting to be supporters or followers) did not behave in an improper, offensive, abusive or insulting way with either an express or implied reference to religion or belief," said an FA statement., external

Chelsea admitted the charge but had an appeal against the fine issued by an independent regulatory commission rejected.

The FA's written reasons stated that although the discriminatory chanting "lasted approximately one minute and was not repeated, the scale of participation was a significant aggravating feature".

"We unequivocally condemn this behaviour," said a Chelsea statement., external "Sectarian abuse - chanting that creates division targeted towards a particular religious or political group - and discriminatory language of any kind has no place in our football club.

"Chelsea takes a zero-tolerance approach towards discriminatory behaviour in whatever form it takes. We will always take steps to identify those responsible and take appropriate action where necessary."

The FA itself was fined by Uefa for a similar incident of chanting, from England's away support during their Nations League victory in Spain on Sunday.

#775. Premier League news: Moyes demands more from Grealish, Iraola wary of United threat

Everton’s playmaker returns after being stood down, while Liverpool’s head coach keeps focus for Anfield showdown

David Moyes has said he wants Jack Grealish to produce more for Everton as he prepares to reintegrate the playmaker into the squad.

Grealish has missed Everton’s past four games mainly for disciplinary reasons having failed to report for training before last month’s Carabao Cup win over Newcastle. His last appearance for the team was in the 2-0 loss to Chelsea on 17 October but he is fit and available for Monday’s visit to Brentford.

“He has served his punishment and we will treat him as we were treating him before,” the Everton manager said. “We will get on with things. The team is doing really well at the moment and what I don’t want to do is turn it into a Jack story because it shouldn’t be.”

The 31-year-old played in a behind-closed-doors fixture against Derby last week andalso apologised on social media for being unable to help the team, who won three of four matches in his absence. Grealish, however, had struggled to replicate last season’s form impact when joining on loan from Manchester City prior to his breach of discipline. And Moyes is demanding more.

He added: “Jack can offer us a lot. I want more from him, I want him to show more than he has done. I want him to give me more assists, more goals. There’s lots of things about him which we need and he’s good at retaining the ball, giving us good possession, carrying. So we hope that he can get back to those levels and give us what we need. I think this time last year he was probably sitting on five or six assists so we’re hoping to get that again.”

The Everton manager has backed Jordan Pickford to respond strongly to the threat from James Trafford to his England place, following after the Leeds goalkeeper’s inclusion and impressive display in the Nations League win over Spain.

“I don’t think it will have a great effect on him,” claimed Moyes. “If you’re playing for England you will always have other players chasing you. I still think Jordan Pickford is out there on his own at the moment. If anything, he’s getting better. It will be good for us now that he’s getting competition [with England].” Andy Hunter

Andoni Iraola has said Liverpool must disregard the latest turmoil at Manchester United and treat Sunday’s visitors like the team that thrived under Michael Carrick last season.

Sunday will be the first time since March 1937 that United have faced Liverpool in a league game at Anfield while languishing in the relegation zone. Mauricio Pochettino could start his United reign bottom of the table should results on Saturday go against his new club.

Iraola never lost in six league meetings with United as Bournemouth head coach. Before his first taste of the fixture with Liverpool, he insisted his north-west rivals are in a false position.

“United finished third in the table last season. You are looking at a squad with exactly the same players. They had very, very good results, especially in the second half of the season,” Iraola said. “Now we have just started, it is just 10 games. For sure, they will be a lot higher in the table [soon]. We have to rate them like this and the truth is the reference we have is that they finished third.

“We have to look at ourselves because we need the points. We need to improve our home form. It is also a big game in terms of relevance. It’s Liverpool v Manchester United, this is the biggest one in English football, so we want to play well and we want to win.”

Iraola was boosted this week by the returns of Conor Bradley and Giovanni Leoni to training after serious knee injuries, although the two defenders are not yet ready for consideration. “We think they will have two weeks on and off with the group,” he said. “Then it is going to be a matter of whether we organise something behind closed doors, 11 v 11, or they straight away play with the under-21s. Before they start playing with us they have to go through that.”

Liverpool’s other long-term absentee, Hugo Ekitiké, remains on course to return in January from an achilles injury. Andy Hunter

Xabi Alonso has admitted Chelsea’s injury list is a concern. The club have a lighter schedule after their failure to qualify for Europe but they are struggling to keep players fit and have a host of selection issues before Saturday’s home game against Leeds.

The Brazil striker João Pedro is yet to return from a thigh injury, Reece James is unlikely to recover from knee surgery until the new year and the France centre-back Maxence Lacroix is out with a long-term hamstring injury. Alonso is having to adjust. Jorrel Hato is unavailable in defence with a back injury and the England Under-21 winger Jamie Gittens, who has made five league starts for Chelsea since joining for £51.5m in the summer of 2025, has been out since September.

“It’s a concern,” Alonso said of the injuries. “Sometimes you can analyse them and find a reason but sometimes it is difficult to find a reason.”

Alonso has made 24 changes to his lineup in his first 10 league games. “It depends on the context and adaptability. I adapt to the circumstances. With the injuries you don’t have a choice. Once you have the whole menu, you can select what you like and I know what I like from the menu.”

Chelsea have failed to score in three of the four league games João Pedro has missed this season. They have also had to monitor Moisés Caicedo closely, with the midfielder minding a muscle issue. But Alonso wants his side to become less reliant on Caicedo and João Pedro.

“We want to have a complete squad,” he said. “That’s the goal of any manager. We have built a good squad. We are a better team with them. But it’s not about making a big drama when someone is out.” Jacob Steinberg

Enzo Maresca has said he may need to tweak the balance of Manchester City’s midfield amid their faltering Premier League form.

City went into the November international break on the back of three consecutive defeats in the league, having begun the campaign with seven wins on the bounce. Maresca’s side are third in the table, six points off leaders Arsenal, and face Fulham at the Etihad Stadium on Saturday.

Maresca defended Enzo Fernández, whose performances have prompted debate over his best position and whether he leaves City’s team unbalanced. Maresca has mostly opted to play the £125m signing from Chelsea deeper in midfield alongside fellow summer recruit Elliot Anderson, with the more defensive-minded Ayyoub Bouaddi, who also arrived in the summer, largely a substitute.

“For sure there are things we need to do better in terms of balance,” Maresca said. “But the same midfield that won seven games in a row is the same midfield that lost three games in a row.

“We won games with Enzo, we lost games with Enzo. I know that when there is a defeat, we are all looking for the reason why. Sometimes we probably need more balance, we need different kinds of players. [It] depends a little bit on the game. The idea is to continue in attack in the same way, creating chances, but finding a balance when we defend.”

Maresca also dismissed the notion that any uncertainty surrounding City’s financial case with the Premier League has negatively affected recent performances. It has been nearly two months since City were found guilty of more than 100 charges related to breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, and they are waiting for the outcome of their appeal. All three of City’s league defeats have come since the ruling.

“I don’t think the players are thinking too much about the noise,” Maresca said. “I don’t think they are worried about it.” Dominic Booth

#774. EU leaders tussle over whom to send to Ukraine, Russia peace talks

A seat at the table for Europe now appears likely following comments by a US envoy who just held talks with Putin. But who will take that seat remains unclear.

European leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent them in Ukraine peace talks after US envoy Steve Witkoff told reporters that the Europeans will be present at the next meetings.

When asked by DW during the European Political Community summit in Dublin why Europe should only get one seat at the table while the US gets two, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas responded with a wry, ironic laugh ― clearly a sign of the frustration felt by European leaders about being sidelined thus far.

The summit of 47 European leaders in Dublin comes in the wake of a diplomatic tour by two Donald Trump administration advisers, the president's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, to talks in Abu Dhabi, followed by a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

The pair then hot-footed their way to Dublin to debrief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelekenskyy.

Zelenskyy and Kushner also said Thursday that Europeans would be at the table for the next talks with Russia on ending the war.

Kallas is one of the figures tipped as most likely to represent the EU in any future talks to end Russia's war against Ukraine, alongside EU Council President Antonio Costa. As yet, the EU hasn’t been able to land on one central figure to send ― many of the national leaders want to be present themselves.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz insisted Europe will be present.

"At the table must be sitting Ukraine, must be sitting the Europeans, must be sitting the Americans, and naturally Russia," he told reporters in Dublin.

But he, like many other leaders, played down the idea of appointing a special envoy for the talks.

Zelenskyy is insistent on European involvement in the peace talks.

"Not directly yet, and not yet when the Russians are at the table," he told the other leaders during the Dublin meetings. "But Europeans are already involved. And we need to make sure that Europe becomes a regular part of these negotiations."

Europe’s division over exactly who should be present has caused a public battle to erupt. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote an excoriating letter to Costa last week, bemoaning the lack of unity.

"By projecting the image of a Europe that is in disarray, we are merely serving the interests of those who want this war to continue," wrote Meloni.

European leaders had even seemed divided over their level of frustration about the situation.

Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Jansa said in Dublin that it was creating a "bad mood" among leaders, however Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs disputed those comments saying, "I don’t feel that."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The palpable fear among the leaders in Dublin is that the US will accept Russia's demands that Europe changes the way it structures its own security, mainly through the NATO military alliance, in exchange for a seat at the table.

Putin said a commitment that Ukraine will never join NATO and even the potential rolling back of the alliance to remove new joiners Finland and Sweden, could be among his demands.

"What do we hear from them [Europeans]?" asked Putin during the meeting with Kushner and Witkoff in Moscow. "That once a peace agreement is signed, they will immediately deploy troops in Ukraine. This is a legitimate target for us, so the war will resume immediately."

This is exactly the kind of rhetoric the European leaders say they are most wary of, especially those in Russia’s direct neighborhood.

"Right now, we are in the [Russian] trap," said Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal. "If something is a threat to you, will you discuss your defense with the threat [itself]?"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US President Donald Trump said publicly that he was hoping for a "very big, beautiful agreement" that "might involve all of Europe."

Zelensky said he found the US approach "a bit strange."

Many of Europe's leaders speaking in Dublin referenced previous agreements with Russia that they believe Moscow has breached.

They include the 1975 Helsinki Accords, the 1990 Paris Charter, 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act and the one they consider most important: the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, which forbids Russia from using force against Ukraine unless in self-defense.

The rancor over the seat at the peace talks is drawing focus away from arguably the bigger battle in the EU now ― how to fund Ukraine as the war continues.

Back in October, the European Commission identified a €70 billion hole in the EU’s funding it had promised for Ukraine’s economy.

Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico has opposed any further financial and military support for Ukraine.

But Germany's Merz warned he could block the EU's next seven-year budget unless member states agree to contribute to Ukraine's financing.

#772. 10 games, 0 points & 30 goals conceded - why Charlton are struggling

Ashleigh Neville joined Charlton from Leicester City in the summer

Charlton Athletic achieved the unthinkable last season when they earned promotion to the Women's Super League - but it has been a harsh introduction.

After 10 games in the top flight, Karen Hills' side are yet to pick up a point and have scored just five goals, conceding 30.

They have already lost to the other promoted sides - Birmingham City and Crystal Palace - and are six points adrift at the bottom of the table.

The club expected a tough challenge as they made the jump up to the WSL for the first time but the results have still hit them hard.

"I'm trying everything I can," manager Hills said following their 2-0 defeat by West Ham last weekend.

That result came a week after Charlton's 3-2 loss at Crystal Palace where they had been leading with 16 minutes to go.

So is it time to consider relegation, even in November, or is there still hope for Charlton to turn things around?

Charlton pipped better resourced teams in the WSL 2 last season, eventually beating top-flight side Leicester City in a play-off to secure promotion.

An incredible 27-game unbeaten run ended in March but was founded on an effective defensive structure and often heroics by goalkeeper Sophie Whitehouse.

However, the step up has proved difficult with inexperience and tight finances standing in the way.

Statistically, Charlton rank bottom in the WSL for average possession (30%), shots on target (17), passing accuracy (66%) and successful passes (1,689).

They have conceded nine times from set-pieces - the most in the WSL - and 14 of their total goals against have come in either the first or final 15 minutes in games.

The only other sides to lose their first 10 games in a WSL season are Doncaster Rovers Belles in 2016 and Yeovil Town in 2017-18. The Belles went on to win just one game as they were relegated, while Yeovil failed to win any, drawing two and finishing bottom, only avoiding relegation because of a league restructure.

Experienced defender Ashleigh Neville, who joined Charlton from Leicester City in the summer, told BBC Sport: "We knew it was going to be a tough start to the season.

"I was really excited to embrace that challenge. It's been difficult with results but when you look at the first game compared to now, I'd like to hope that people can see we're trying to build something.

"We're trying the hardest we can off the pitch to get to terms with how quick the game is compared to the WSL 2 and the quality of players we're up against.

"But it's still a joy to come into work and people are wanting to be better, asking how they can improve and move forward."

This month, manager Hills insisted Charlton "will never throw the towel in" but admitted results are "hurting" the club.

Neville added: "It is not at the forefront of things but we've been really unlucky with the injuries that we've had in our attacking line.

"We're lacking in confidence going forward, and creativity for what we can actually provide.

"It's a vicious circle. If you haven't got confidence because you're losing games, how do you still get that confidence in games where we need it the most?"

Whitehouse's penalty masterclass sends Charlton into WSL

How WSL 2 title contenders Charlton are defying the odds

Karen Hills was a player at Charlton Athletic before retiring in 2007

Charlton are one of only three clubs without Premier League male counterparts to offer financial backing in the WSL and that restricts their freedom in recruitment.

It has not helped that summer signing Linda Lif Boama suffered a serious knee injury in September, defender Grace Johnston was ruled out in October and Paula Partido had to return to parent club London City Lionesses for knee surgery.

Charlotte Newsham, who played a key role in their WSL 2 promotion run, was also sidelined by an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury before the play-off victory.

While Charlton sought out shrewd signings in the summer, rivals Birmingham City were able to spend six-figure sums on Manchester United duo Lisa Naalsund and Millie Turner.

The Blues also broke their club record in January - a reported Â£316,000 fee for Wilma Leidhammar - while Oceane Hurtre was signed last summer to boost their second-tier title hopes and has now scored seven goals in 10 WSL games.

Fellow promoted club Palace picked up four-time WSL winner Bethany England and one of the WSL 2's standout players Lexi Lloyd-Smith in the summer.

"WSL 2 teams have to be even more ready for the WSL while they're still in the WSL 2 so that when they do make that jump, it's not a huge gap," said Hills.

"The gap is continuing to get bigger and you see some of the players the top teams have brought in and the finances they have.

"It's a big challenge for us. We're finding that out on a weekly basis."

Charlton benefited from the WSL's expansion this summer to 14 teams from 12 as organisers try to bridge the gap between the leagues and to increase the number of matches.

It was well-received by fans and those within the game, but Hills says it will still take time for WSL 2 clubs to catch up.

"If you look at the bottom three teams [in the table], it's all the newly-promoted teams. The level that we're coming into is already very well established."

Neville added: "I think the financial side plays a massive part. We do our bit where we can. But it's hard to bring in the experienced players you need."

#771. Pochettino the connector: will human touch lift Manchester United?

Argentinian has excelled in man-management – but will need his powers to energise new squad and impress owners

Mauricio Pochettino celebrated his 50th birthday in style. It was March 2022, he was in charge at Paris Saint-Germain and the venue was a stunning boutique hotel; the kind that many capitals have but only Paris truly does. Pochettino’s family and friends were there. So were his inner coaching circle, who are basically family. There were lots of people from PSG. And a good time was had by all.

For Pochettino, it was emotional. As everybody knows, the new Manchester United head coach is the kind of guy to well up when the speeches start, so imagine how he felt when he looked up at the big screen and a video montage of well-wishers started to roll.

Pochettino’s PSG players were at the party. There was no need for anything from them. But there were loads from those he had coached at his previous clubs: Espanyol, Southampton and Tottenham. One by one, the faces flashed up; too many to mention. And, of course, there were the jokes about how old he was getting. But the tone was of pure affection; appreciation, too. Some of the players laid it on thick. They could not help it. They know what Pochettino has done for them.

This is what total buy-in looks like and this is how Pochettino gets you when he finds out which buttons to press. It might be a third-choice goalkeeper. Or a global superstar – for example, Kylian Mbappé, who Pochettino had at PSG. There is a story from those days that is worth sharing. Pochettino was due to give an interview and told the TV crew he would get Mbappé along to speak to them as well.

Everybody knows this is not how it works, that it would not be possible because Mbappé, well … he has his time and commitments tightly managed. They appreciated the sentiment from Pochettino, though. When the hour came, Pochettino took out his phone and messaged Mbappé. “Come to the media centre.” Five minutes later, there he was. A line from one of the production staff was gold. “Err, we’ve got Kylian Mbappé outside.”

This kind of thing is not confined to the dim and distant past. Remember when Pochettino left Chelsea in 2024 and the tributes some of the players paid to him on social media? One stood out because it came from Nicolas Jackson, who Pochettino had punished for getting too many silly yellow cards by ordering him to sprint around the training ground, reducing him to a face-in-the-ground mess when it was over. “Love you coach,” Jackson wrote. “Thanks for the advice and support. You’re a true lion and a fighter.”

It is easy to feel Pochettino has signed up for his biggest fight because it is not only that United have one Premier League win, a place in the relegation zone, no confidence, questionable fitness levels and a trip to Liverpool on Sunday which has the makings of root canal surgery without the anaesthetic.

Hanging heavy over everything is the fan fury towards the Glazer family, who have owned the club since 2005. It is obviously not a new thing. The diehards were passionately against them even before the takeover. But we are going through another period where the frustration has spiked and the malevolence can be heard in the chants. It is the insoluble problem, with the efforts of the minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the director of football, Jason Wilcox, making it worse. They have also been targeted by the Stretford End.

Pochettino knows managers do not tend to enter clubs when everything is rosy. There are reasons why the vacancies arise and they are almost always bad. He has told himself this. What he intends to do is what he has always done: create connections, starting with the players; inject his trademark positivity into every pore; build belief.

The Argentinian is obsessed with what he calls energia universal. It is a guiding life force that influences everything, which touches on concepts such as karma and what these days would probably be called manifestation. He once said it helped to explain, for example, why the London-born Harry Kane usually scored for Spurs in London derbies.

Pochettino wants to release the pressure from United’s beleaguered squad and his early messaging has come from his tried and trusted playbook. He will treat each player as a human being, first and foremost, with individual needs. And, if necessary, individually tailored programmes. At Southampton, he put one together for Luke Shaw, then an emerging player. He has been reunited with the left-back at Old Trafford.

Pochettino talked at his media conference on Friday of having had three hours of one-on-one meetings with the players on Thursday; trying to understand what was happening with them on and off the field. Previously, in his opening address to the United fanbase via the club’s in-house channels, he stressed the importance of everybody “connecting together”.

“The responsibility I feel is energy, it’s excitement,” he said. “To connect with the game we need to feel free. The players need to express their talent and we need to create the environment for them to perform. That is the priority.”

Pochettino has been close to the United job before – most notably in the summer of 2022 when he left PSG. It was either him or Erik ten Hag to take over from the interim Ralf Rangnick, who had declared that United needed “open-heart surgery”. What do they need now?! The club went for Ten Hag.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Pochettino was in United’s thoughts when they looked for a successor to Louis van Gaal in May 2016; he had lunch with Sir Alex Ferguson at Scott’s in London that month. It was believed Ferguson was pushing him as a candidate. United appointed José Mourinho. There was also the period after Mourinho’s dismissal in December 2018 and the interim hire of Ole Gunnar Solskjær when Pochettino was tipped to go to Old Trafford. In the end, Solskjær earned the role on a permanent basis.

Why are United turning now to a manager they have previously overlooked? Pochettino is not about to dwell on that because he is in dream-come-true territory. He will love how the United support stand behind their manager, especially in troublesome times. He will love the pageantry and event glamour of Old Trafford. And he will love having Ferguson in the crowd for the matches.

Pochettino first encountered him in January 2013 when, in his second Southampton game, he went to Old Trafford to face Ferguson’s United, who won 2-1. Pochettino has mentioned that this week. And the meal at Scott’s. And how he was at the Camp Nou for Ferguson’s finest hour: the 1999 Champions League final victory against Bayern Munich. Pochettino was an Espanyol player at the time, together with Toni Jiménez, who is part of his coaching staff, and they watched the first half from so-so seats before blagging their way into the directors’ box for the second period.

When Solskjær scored his iconic late winner, Pochettino and Jiménez celebrated wildly. They were caught up in the moment. It was the first time Pochettino felt a connection to United and he began to pay more attention to them. And Ferguson. Pochettino described him this week as “the best coach in the history of the sport” but it was not a soundbite of convenience. He has always maintained this and said so on the record after the lunch at Scott’s.

How can Pochettino position himself in terms of the Glazers and Ratcliffe? The first thing to say is that he does have experience of unpopular and/or difficult owners. At Spurs, Daniel Levy was forever maligned by the fans, and Pochettino had problems with the American ownership at Chelsea. Between times, the Qataris at PSG were not easy. Pochettino worked to build a relationship with Levy, regularly saying nice things about him in the press and famously including him on a staff-bonding trip to Argentina.

It featured white-water rafting and ended with Pochettino having to fish Levy out of the Manso River. A repeat of the adventure with Joel Glazer feels unlikely but Pochettino’s starting point at United has been to stress unity; the need to create chemistry with everyone, including “the directors and the owners”.

And so to Anfield, where Pochettino first managed with Southampton in September 2013 when his team won 1-0. He has not tasted victory in his eight subsequent trips; seven with Spurs, one with Chelsea, the record shows two draws and six defeats. No United fan expects anything this time but Pochettino considers it a great game to have. He will certainly learn a lot about his players.

#770. Filming training by drones should be illegal - Iraola

Andoni Iraola's Liverpool take on Mauricio Pochettino's Manchester United on Sunday

Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola says filming with drones around training grounds should be illegal after Mauricio Pochettino's first session as Manchester United boss was captured and uploaded online.

Pochettino and his players were clearly visible in the footage, which was shot above United's Carrington training base from a variety of angles and distances.

The drone operater apologised and later took down the footage, with sources telling BBC Sport they are adamant there was no security breach and that they do not intend to take legal action.

Iraola said he was sent the 12 minutes of footage on Thursday - three days before United travel to Anfield for a Premier League match.

"The important part of this is that it shouldn't be legal," he said on Friday. "It happened to United but it could happen to me.

"Yesterday, when Sky Sports had access to our training and the cameras recorded 15-20 minutes, you know who trained and who didn't.

"It's not the matter of the advantage. It's the fact that someone can do this. There's a reason we train behind closed doors because there are some things that you have to respect. I don't think it's nice for any club."

Filming training on a drone 'shouldn't be legal' - Iraola

Ten outfield players were seen working directly with former United States boss Pochettino in the footage, though it seems unlikely they will all start Sunday's match.

"We've faced each other and obviously he [Pochettino] has a lot of Premier League games behind him that we can look at," said Iraola.

"We can look at games from the US but it's true that they have this small advantage that we don't have references to prepare, because they can go different ways that we honestly don't know right now."

Iraola said he expected United to be "well prepared" as Pochettino's assistants travelled to England to work with the players before the Argentine arrived on Wednesday.

"They have this advantage that we don't exactly know - or at least we don't have the references like we do against other opposition," he said.

"Especially the beginning of the game will be important. We have to adapt to certain things. But we know the players very well."

Liverpool are fourth in the table - 14 places ahead of United.

But they have failed to beat the Red Devils at Anfield in each of the past three seasons, and have lost to Arsenal and Manchester City at home already in this campaign.

"You don't find bigger games than this," said Iraola. "I feel lucky to be here and privileged to be a part of these games.

"We have to acknowledge the importance of the game. There are a lot of ingredients. They have a new manager, new challenges for us. This is important for us in a lot of different ways.

"We want to improve our form at home. We have been very good away but not good at home and the first chance we have is United on Sunday."

#769. Lampard calls for fairness after Coventry penalty row

This is Coventry's first season in the Premier League with video assistant referee reviews

Frustrated Frank Lampard has called for fairness from officials after Coventry were denied a clear penalty - with the boss claiming it got less coverage because they are a smaller club.

The Sky Blues were furious they were not awarded a first-half spot kick in the 3-1 defeat at Everton before the international break.

James Tarkowski pulled Caleb Yirenkyi's hair in the area but was not penalised by referee Stuart Attwell or video assistant referee (VAR) Timothy Wood.

The Key Match Incidents Panel, which assesses the contentious incidents and whether the officials got them correct, this week voted unanimously that the Sky Blues should have been awarded a penalty.

It would have given Coventry a chance to go 1-0 up, before Yann Gboho fired them ahead early in the second half - only for Everton to recover.

Thierno Barry scored twice, and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall added the third for the hosts but Lampard also argued because the decisions went against Coventry they were not given the same scrutiny as others.

"I'm not sure how much coverage it got in the days after, maybe because we're Coventry, move on everybody," said Lampard, with defeat leaving them 17th in the Premier League.

"We lost a game and we move on but we need fairness.

"If the decision is rightly for us give it to us, I'm not asking for anything beyond that.

"We're not asking for anything beyond fairness to get the right decision, to spend enough time on the decision. We're fighting on so many levels here as a promoted club.

"We've been out of the league for 25 years, we've got a lack of experience in the squad because the boys that have come up haven't played in the Premier League.

"Financially what we do in the league, in terms of where we are and the wages, we know we're right at the bottom and all these things, so we're fighting for every moment and we're grafting a lot and you just really do want that fairness."

Taiwo Awoniyi appeared to be brought down on the edge of the box by Vitalii Mykolenko

Coventry also felt they could have had a penalty when Taiwo Awoniyi was tripped by Vitalii Mykolenko early in the second half and that Everton striker Thierno Barry handled the ball before scoring his crucial second goal.

Pro Ref chief executive Howard Webb has spoken with Lampard and Coventry sporting director Dean Austin over the decisions, with Webb acknowledging the wrong decision over the hair pull.

The hair pulling guidance was relaxed in the summer with referees advised it would not necessarily mean a straight red card, although sources accept the softening of guidance could lead to more grey areas at times - something Lampard disputed in this instance.

"There was no grey area with this, they missed it. They watched the video and they missed it," said Lampard, before Saturday's visit of Crystal Palace.

"They watched it for a good minute and a half. I've seen it and I've heard the footage. They missed it completely.

"I got fined once for talking about a referee as manager of Everton and I hate talking about it but when you work for the club you feel the pain yourself.

"You fight all week for a result and there's something with real clarity that can't really be missed. The Tarkowski one, it can't be missed at this level.

"So that's quite hard to take as well because we all saw it on the Sky broadcast pretty much straight away. So I respect and appreciate Howard Webb saying that to myself and Dean in a meeting afterwards.

"I like that side of things. Howard Webb was, when I was playing, one of the best referees in the world and I think he's very good at his job. He was upfront about the fact they missed it."

#768. Iranian activist and Nobel Peace Prize winner Narges Mohammadi shares her story in memoir

Written and smuggled out of prison, the 2023 Nobel Prize laureate's memoir reveals the cost of defying Iran's regime and fighting for freedom.

As PEN International marks Imprisoned Writer Day on November 15, a memoir by 2023 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi stands as a powerful act of resistance against authoritarian regimes.

"A Woman Never Stops Fighting — My Struggle for Freedom, Democracy and Human Rights in Iran," was recently published in German and is set to be released in English in September 2027.

The autobiography "portrays how Narges actually became the woman she is today — and it also reveals the price she had to pay to become that woman," Mariam Claren, spokesperson for the Narges Mohammadi Foundation Germany told DW.

Mohammadi wrote the autobiography in prison: "She was constantly writing," says Claren, whose own mother, activist Nahid Taghavi, shared a cell with Mohammadi for two and a half years, in Iran's notorious Evin prison. "Then, in 2020, Narges was forcibly moved to another prison. All her documents were gone. And she had to start all over."

But she managed to rewrite it all, and her texts were smuggled out of prison in fragments by fellow prisoners and visitors who risked their own safety.

In her memoir, Mohammadi recounts pivotal moments in her life, including her childhood and youth, how she started taking action against gender discrimination, political repression, the death penalty and human rights abuses, and the personal and emotional toll of her activism.

The human rights activist has been sentenced to a combined total of more than 44 years in prison and 154 lashes. For more than a decade, she has been separated from her twin children, who are now 19 years old and live in exile in France for their own protection.

Born on April 21, 1972, in Zanjan, Iran, Narges Mohammadi became politically active while studying in physics at Imam Khomeini University of Qazvin in the 1990s.

In "A Woman Never Stops Fighting," she describes how she started mountain climbing as a student, and organized mixed-gender groups dedicated to mountaineering — a controversial initiative at the time. She also helped establish an independent student organization and advocated for political reform. Her activities led to repeated harassment and arrests by authorities.

She began her journalism career in 1996, writing about Iran's student and women's movements. As her public profile grew, she became increasingly involved in Iran's civil society and human rights community.

In 1998, she married political activist Taghi Rahmani. The couple's twins, Ali and Kiana, were born in 2006.

Over the course of her career, Mohammadi worked with some of Iran's most prominent human rights organizations and became a leading figure in the Defenders of Human Rights Centre, founded by 2003 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Shirin Ebadi.

She played a key role in initiatives promoting free elections, peace and the abolition of the death penalty, especially for juvenile offenders. She also helped establish organizations supporting political prisoners and advocating for women's rights.

Her first major prison sentence related to her human rights activities came in 2011. It marked the beginning of a cycle of arrests and prosecutions that would define much of her adult life.

In her memoir, she describes an arrest that took place in front of her young children. At one point during her imprisonment, she lost the right to call them for several months.

She also details the brutal treatment she experienced in prison, with constant interrogations, beatings and denial of medical care.

Another central focus of her activism is denouncing the psychological effects of solitary confinement, which she had previously documented with fellow inmates in her book and documentary project "White Torture."

"When someone is subjected to physical torture, the scars, blood and infections — dreadful as they may be — serve as visible witnesses," she writes in her memoir. But, she adds, "when someone is subjected to psychological torture, no visible traces remain, and the victim cannot justify the trauma — neither to themselves nor to others. In fact, it becomes virtually impossible to even accept that one has been tortured at all, which causes the suffering to continue indefinitely."

"This is also the goal of solitary confinement: to bring the imprisoned person to the very edge of nothingness — to strip them of their identity and of everything that makes them human," she writes.

Through her relentless campaigning against executions and state violence, she helped bring these issues to the forefront of public debate among Iranian activists.

International recognition of her work culminated in October 2023 when she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for "for her fight against the oppression of women in Iran and her fight to promote human rights and freedom for all."

As Mohammadi was unable to attend the ceremony because she remained imprisoned in Tehran's Evin Prison, the award was accepted on her behalf by her teenage twins, who delivered her message to the world.

Following the Nobel Prize, Iranian authorities continued to pursue new legal cases against her, restrict her communications and intensify pressure on her from prison.

She became the target of a systematic smear campaign, including widespread defamation, gender-based harassment and explicit death threats.

"We are firmly convinced that the Islamic Republic of Iran has deployed its cyber army — which is the second-largest, after Russia's — to this end," says Claren of the Narges Mohammadi Foundation. Conspiracy theorists even started claiming she might be working for the regime, she adds: "And what is truly terrible about this is that when a lie is repeated over and over again and spread over the course of years, it eventually leads even ordinary people to start believing it."

In late 2024, following surgery, Mohammadi was granted a temporary medical release. Doctors warned at the time that a return to prison could seriously endanger her health.

Nevertheless, Mohammadi was brutally arrested again in December 2025, while attending a memorial ceremony for Khosrow Alikordi, a lawyer and human rights activist who died in suspicious circumstances.

In prison, she was held in solitary confinement for an extended period and her health continued to deteriorate, Claren reports. But "thanks to a public campaign, she has now been granted what is known as an interruption of detention for medical reasons."

But "that doesn't mean she is free," adds Claren, who notes that she still suffers from serious health problems — as do many Iranians who have been tortured in prison.

In February, an Iranian court ordered additional prison sentences for Mohammadi, along with a travel ban.

Mohammadi lives in constant fear of having to return to prison any day, notes Claren, and "this all comes with the pressure to which Iranian civil society — including, of course, people like Narges — is currently subjected, with questions like: Will Trump launch an attack, yes or no? Will there be another war?"

Despite this uncertainty, Mohammadi continues her activism. Her international profile also helps her supporters keep addressing publicly the issue of human rights in Iran in the public eye, says Claren: "It is incredibly important that, alongside the individual Narges Mohammadi, the focus also remains consistently on the struggle of the people in Iran for freedom, dignity, and fundamental rights — for the right to sing and dance."

#767. Bayern Munich confirm Harry Kane ‘out for next few months’ with ankle injury

England forward injured in Friday’s 1-1 draw with Cologne

Club statement confirms ‘tear of ligament in left ankle’

Bayern Munich have confirmed Harry Kane will be “out for the next few months” with ankle ligament damage sustained in their 1-1 draw with Cologne on Friday.

Kane was substituted after 20 minutes of the Bundesliga game, having been left limping after a challenge from the Cologne defender Joël Schmied. The Ballon d’Or winner was substituted and the returning Bayern coach, Vincent Kompany, said that the injury would take “months” rather than weeks to heal.

A club statement on X said: “Harry Kane suffered a tear of the syndesmosis ligament in his left ankle in Bayern Munich’s Bundesliga home match against Köln on Friday evening. This was confirmed by an examination by Bayern Munich’s medical department. The 33-year-old will therefore be out for the next few months.”

The Tottenham loanee Mikey Moore fired the visitors ahead before Kane’s injury, but Bayern levelled when Nathaniel Brown scored before the break. Bayern also lost Michael Olise to injury for the second half, and Said El Mala missed an excellent late chance to earn Cologne’s first win at Bayern since 2009.

The 33-year-old may face a race to be fit for the Nations League quarter-finals, the first leg of which takes place in Norway on 27 March – just over four months away. The Bayern sporting director, Max Eberl, said on Friday that club doctors were “discussing whether or not to recommend surgery” for Kane’s injury.

Part of Kane’s recovery period will come during the Bundesliga’s winter break from 20 December to 8 January. He will, however, miss Champions League games away to Lille next week and at home to Slavia Prague next month, as well as the January trip to Manchester United and the league phase finale at home to Real Betis.

Kane’s setback adds to an extensive Bayern injury list, with Olise also going off during Friday’s game with a foot contusion. Luis Díaz, Serge Gnabry, Alphonso Davies, Ismael Saibari and Manuel Neuer were already unavailable, leaving Kompany short of options for a busy month of fixtures.

Kompany returned from his own month-long absence for Friday’s game with his arm in a sling, having dislocated his shoulder when he collapsed on a training pitch in October. The Belgian was taken to hospital for meningeal irritation treatment after his collapse, and has been recovering at home.

“I think this result was fair and Cologne deserved the point,” Kompany said after the game. “We have other worries now, I have to honestly say. We will all try together to make something strong out of this situation. FC Bayern does that time and again, and that’s what we want to do now too.”

Cologne took a surprise lead with 12 minutes gone when Moore started and finished an excellent break. The teenage winger pounced on a mislaid Olise pass and drove forward, finding Linton Maina who laid off for El Mala, whose no-look backheel pass allowed Moore to round keeper Jonas Urbig before sliding the ball home.

Kane was then brought down in the Cologne box from behind by Schmied, who got the ball first but clattered into Kane’s left leg in his follow-through. Kane’s penalty appeals were waved away, but he was left visibly limping and received treatment on his ankle before being replaced by Tom Bischof on the 20-minute mark.

The hosts levelled 17 minutes later when full-back Brown sliced a low shot into the bottom-right corner, but suffered another blow just before the break when Olise went down. The France star did not return for the second half and was seen leaving the stadium shortly after on crutches – but it appears unlikely he will miss a significant amount of time.

Just before the hour mark, El Mala and Maina forced a spectacular double save from Urbig. El Mala, recently called up by Germany, then had a golden chance to put Cologne in front with eight minutes to go when one-on-one with Urbig – but he cut his close-range shot inches wide of the post.

Now a point behind Bayern, Borussia Dortmund can move into outright first place if they win at bottom club Mönchengladbach on Saturday. Freiburg can also move level on points with Bayern if they can defeat promoted Elversberg.

This month Kane signed a new deal with the Bundesliga giants until June 2029, which is reportedly worth in excess of £400,000 a week, making him the highest-paid player in Europe before bonuses.

Since arriving from Tottenham three years ago, Kane has scored an incredible 156 goals in 163 appearances, helping Bayern win a league and cup double last season.

#766. Arteta warns Arsenal players over FPL team news leak

Arsenal currently sit top of the Premier League, five points clear of Brighton in second

Mikel Arteta says his Arsenal players have been warned against inadvertently leaking team news via Fantasy Premier League.

The intervention comes after Christos Tzolis selected and captained himself in his Fantasy Premier League (FPL) team before Arsenal's match against Liverpool on 1 November, after he had missed a month through injury.

The Gunners manager picked the winger in Arsenal's starting XI at Anfield in what was his first appearance since Greece's Nations League draw with the Netherlands on 1 October.

Before Saturday's match at Newcastle, Arteta said he had to speak to his squad, and those close to the club, about their FPL selections.

"With Christos, with the squad and with my kids as well," he said

"They're constantly asking me about this as well, because they want to know. It's a topic.

"This is the kind of thing that is happening in our society right now. It's something new. We haven't dealt with it before and we need to put new things in place.

"Obviously, confidentiality is something critical because it's about trust and about what you are trying to do and that should be kept as a huge secret. We'll take measures to make sure it doesn't happen."

The Spaniard also said his players are restricted from selecting themselves in their FPL line-ups.

In October, a number of FPL teams connected to staff and players at Chelsea removed striker Joao Pedro from their teams, hinting the Brazilian had sustained an injury.

#765. Man Utd fan criticism has gone too far at times - Berrada

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada (left) with director of football Jason Wilcox

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada says some of the criticism aimed at the club's hierarchy has "crossed a line".

In a rare interview to Sky Sports as head coach Mauricio Pochettino prepares for his first game in charge, at Liverpool on Sunday, Berrada said he "understood" the frustration of supporters at United being 18th in the Premier League. He also said some of the criticism was "fair".

However, he feels some of it has gone too far.

"Being in this position comes naturally with the criticism and scrutiny we're going to get," he said. "We accept it. Some of it is fair, some of it does cross the line.

"We do live in this world of social media, where people like to generate negative stories about the club because it drives more engagement, and it drives more general noise and activity around the club. But we park that."

United's director of football Jason Wilcox has been singled out by supporters at recent games. There have also been social media calls for both Wilcox and Berrada to lose their jobs.

In addition, songs are now sung regularly calling for minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe to leave, while opposition to the Glazer family has remained intense since their leveraged buyout in 2005 saddled debt on to the club that now exceeds Â£1bn.

Cost of Man Utd hiring and firing managers nears Â£100m

Andrey Santos has started four Premier League games for Manchester United since his Â£50m summer move from Chelsea

Wilcox, in particular, has been blamed for what is perceived to have been poor summer recruitment. After the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid in September, defender Lisandro Martinez said he "expected more from the technical director".

Ousted boss Michael Carrick felt he was let down by a transfer strategy that targeted midfield, while not addressing issues at left-back and in attack - which has been compounded by injuries to Luke Shaw and Benjamin Sesko.

Carrick wanted to target Elliot Anderson and Mateus Fernandes, but United backed off when Nottingham Forest and West Ham's demands went higher than they wanted to pay. Anderson eventually joined Manchester City for Â£116m, with Fernandes moving to Tottenham for Â£85m.

Instead, United paid a combined Â£118m for Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos, who have started seven Premier League games between then, and triggered Youri Tielemans' Â£35m release clause at Aston Villa. Tielemans scored his first United goal in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on 8 November and has one assist.

However, Berrada has defended United's transfer business, saying: "When we look at the summer transfer window of 2026, I know we're receiving a lot of criticism for it, but we're actually happy with the players we bought.

"We think that Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos, and Karl Darlow - and let's not forget that we've also welcomed back Marcus Rashford, who had a very good season on loan at Barcelona - these are five additions that we think have made the squad fundamentally better.

"We went in knowing what we needed to do. Of course, there have been different dynamics at play and we've said consistently in the last few years we need to stay disciplined. We need to take the right decisions. We need to buy the right players, for the right value at the right time - in terms of what the squad needs.

"When we find the right opportunities, we will spend. But what we don't want to be doing is spending just for the sake of it. So, could we have signed an additional defender to straighten the depth and the quality? Yes, but we have to find the right players at the right value.

"There's no point in us spending Â£40m, Â£50m for players we're not convinced are going to add value to the team."

When he spoke to the wider media for the first time, 30 minutes before Berrada's interview was aired, Pochettino said he hoped to have a say in all areas of the playing side, even though his official title is head coach.

"I know that, being a head coach, I am the guy that is going to decide the squad for Sunday," he said. "I'm going to pick the starting 11 and I'm going to make the changes.

"Of course, in the future, I would like to be involved in all the main decisions that will happen on the squad."

Berrada said there had been little option other than to dismiss Carrick given United's plight and the team had "dropped off in many areas".

Pochettino has spoken individually to virtually every player to get an understanding of what the issues are.

He said he was wary of reading too much into data that shows United's players have not been running enough, arguing "if you don't put context on the data, it's very dangerous to talk".

The 54-year-old also said that, despite talking extensively about culture in his first in-house interview on Thursday, it could take 10 years to build one.

"The culture of the club and the identity of the club is very clear," he said. "It's a historic club, one of the best in the world. It's difficult to find another club the size of Manchester United.

"The culture of the club and the identity of the club is very clear. It needs to be in a different place than we are now."

Pochettino did confirm Bruno Fernandes will remain as skipper for the trip to Liverpool.

Fernandes has struggled for form and, with the 32-year-old's contract due to expire in the summer, there has been no breakthrough in negotiations over an extension.

United do have the option to trigger an additional year on the Portugal playmaker's present deal but, given the massive dip from the levels that earned him all last season's major player of the year awards, there are some who wonder whether a clean break might be best.

Pochettino preferred to deflect the wider aspect of Fernandes' future and concentrate on the immediate.

"Bruno is our captain and he's a very important player," he said.

"I think we will have time after to talk about the [other] things that you are asking me."

"Starship V4 will be ~70m long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load," the SpaceX CEO said.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As usual, SpaceX and its founder Elon Musk are thinking big.

The company recovered the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever on Saturday (Nov. 14), plucking it out of the sky with the "chopstick" arms of its Texas launch tower.

It was a huge moment for SpaceX, bringing its vision of full and rapid rocket reuse much closer to reality. But Elon Musk isn't one to dwell on the past or rest on laurels, so he soon outlined an even more ambitious future for Starship.

"Starship V4 will be ~70m [230 feet] long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load," Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Sunday evening (Nov. 15). "Engine count will be raised to 9, with 3 more Raptor-Vacuum engines added, and these will be higher-thrust V4 engines."

The current version of Starship — the one that launched Friday (Nov. 13) on the vehicle's 15th test flight — is the V3. It's the largest and most powerful rocket ever built, standing 408 feet (124 m) tall when fully stacked with its Super Heavy first stage and Ship upper stage.

V3's Ship is 171 feet (52 m) tall and features six of SpaceX's Raptor V3 engines. (The similarly reusable Super Heavy V3 booster is powered by 33 Raptors.) So, as Musk noted in his post, the V4 Ship will be quite an upgrade in size and power.

Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon.

Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g.

To provide a little perspective about that vehicle's planned dimensions: The V4 Ship will be the same height as a fully stacked Falcon 9, SpaceX's workhorse two-stage rocket, and much broader: Ship is 30 feet (9 m) across, while the Falcon 9's payload fairing is 17.1 feet (5.2 m) wide.

This isn't the first we've heard about a V4 Starship. Back in August 2025, for example, Musk posted a graphic showing Starship's planned progression from the V2 to the V3 to the V4, which he said is expected to debut in 2027.

That slide pegs the future Starship's total height at 466 feet (142 m), 200 feet (61 m) of which would be Ship. But those numbers are out of date, Musk stressed in the post, saying that V4 is "probably closer to 150m height."

So, yeah: If all goes according to plan, the next Starship will be nearly 500 feet tall.

Starship V4 will be ~70m long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load. Engine count will be raised to 9, with 3 more Raptor-Vacuum engines added, and these will be higher thrust V4 engines.November 16, 2026

The original Starship Flight 15 mission plan called for a double chopsticks catch, with both Super Heavy and Ship coming back to the launch tower for recovery.

This would have been feasible, as the catches were scheduled a day apart: Super Heavy would land just 6.5 minutes after launch, while Ship would circle Earth for 22.5 hours, and deploy a batch of SpaceX's Starlink V3 internet satellites, before coming home. (Ship ended up delivering the satellites as planned.)

The twofer didn't happen, however; Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel alarm and diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday as a result. But that wasn't a huge deal, as SpaceX had already pulled off Super Heavy catches on three previous Starship flights.

The Ship catch was unprecedented, because it's been a taller order. Ship returns to Earth from orbit, so it comes in faster and hotter. SpaceX hadn't even tried the maneuver before Flight 15, so executing it was a very big deal.

"That was the missing link," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during the company's Ship-landing webcast on Saturday. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. #763. Could lack of money sink TFFF rainforest fund before it even launches?

The TFFF rainforest fund aims to make forest conservation more profitable than deforestation. But a lack of money may prevent it from getting off the ground.

The world's tropical forests play a vital role in slowing global heating and preserving biodiversity, storing climate-damaging carbon dioxide and providing a home for an extremely large number of species — when they're intact.

More than 140 countries committed to halting global deforestation by the end of the decade at the 2021 UN climate change conference in Glasgow, but five years later logging continues.

In 2024, over 8 million hectares (19 million acres) of forest were lost. And since 1990, nearly 490 million hectares of forest have been wiped out.

More recently, the trend has shifted in the opposite direction. Deforestation in the Amazon region of Brazil decreased by 41% from August 2025 through 2026 to reach its lowest rate since records began.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

To ensure lasting protection, the Tropical Forest Forever Facility was launched in 2025 at the COP30 climate conference in Belem, Brazil.

Because rainforests are so important for the world, the idea behind the fund was to give money to the countries where they are located to help them preserve and protect these ecosystems.

So far, these countries have made more profit through deforestation — for example, by mining natural resources on rainforest land or farming the area.

Starting in 2027, the TFFF is expected to generate the funds needed for rainforest conservation, in part via contributions from various countries. By the end of this year, a total of $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in government capital is due to flow into the fund, mainly in the form of low-interest loans.

In addition, the TFFF is expected to issue bonds to private investors, such as banks and investment firms, to raise additional funds — initially totaling about $40 billion.

Going forward, the plan is for governments to contribute a total of $25 billion to the pot, and for private donors to contribute $100 billion. The fund will then invest this money in international financial markets with the aim of generating profits.

Private investors who purchase TFFF bonds can expect to earn about 5% interest per bond per year, said Felix Finkbeiner, the founder of the German environmental organization Plant-for-the-Planet, where he is responsible for forest conservation and advocacy.

"Private investors' capital is very well protected," Finkbeiner said, adding that any losses the TFFF might incur on the capital markets — for example, if the price of its bonds should fall — would be offset by government funds.

About 2.7% of the TFFF's profits would be set aside for countries with tropical forests.

Countries would receive $4 per year for every hectare of forest that they preserve instead of chopping down. At least 20% of these funds must be allocated to Indigenous peoples and local communities.

According to calculations by the TFFF Watch website, an independent platform launched by Plant-for-the-Planet to track investments, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for example, would receive about $333 million for its 2024 forest stock under this system.

Finkbeiner said the subsidies would be paid only for intact ecosystems and not for timber plantations, with forest areas and their condition mapped and assessed using satellite imagery. Though it can sometimes be difficult to identify plantations accurately on satellite photos, he said, the technology has improved significantly over the last decade.

That means any NGO or external party with access to the satellite data can check the condition of the region, providing further oversight. If forest areas are cleared or damaged, money is deducted from the total.

Another safeguard: If countries don't use the TFFF funds for rainforest conservation, their payments could be frozen for the next few years.

The TFFF is supposed to invest, whenever possible, in government bonds issued by emerging and developing countries. Above all, the idea is not to invest in projects that harm the climate — such as those linked to oil, gas, or coal investments.

The TFFF concept has received plenty of support from environmental organizations, in part because it gives countries in the Global South significantly more sovereignty than traditional forms of development financing.

"For example, if the government of Ghana wants to protect its rainforest today, it usually asks the World Bank for financial assistance — and then the World Bank in [Washington] DC decides whether Ghana is allowed to do so," Finkbeiner said.

The TFFF fund is also designed to be immune to donor countries' backing out in the event of a change in government, for example. Once a contribution is made, the money remains in the fund for 40 years before being paid back.

Continuing protection is also an incentive for countries receiving money from the fund. "When a new government comes into power that wants to cut back a little on climate protection, they will realize: We'll get more money if we protect the rainforest," said Finkbeiner.

For the rainforest fund to actually get off the ground, a total of $10 billion in seed capital must be raised by the end of 2026. So far, the confirmed pledges from countries, NGOs and foundations total only $7.9 billion.

Eight countries have expressed a willingness to contribute so far, including Brazil, Indonesia, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.

Norway, with a pledge of $3 billion, is the largest would-be donor. However, the government in Oslo is willing to honor its commitment only if the agreed-upon total amount is in place by the end of the year.

"This deadline isn't set in stone, but otherwise the Norwegian government will have real trouble getting it through parliament," Finkbeiner said.

Germany's commitment must also still be approved by the parliament. The German government has pledged about €1 billion to the TFFF starting in 2027, to be paid out over 10 years.

Other countries are also considering investing in the TFFF, including Canada, China, South Korea and the United Arab Emirates.

Philanthropic organizations have pledged $88 million to the fund so far, including $73 million announced this week during the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. Finkbeiner remains upbeat.

"Promises like that always come at the last minute," he said. "I'm very optimistic that we'll secure more commitments at the COP — and in the course of December — and that we'll then reach that $10 billion."
