#632. Germany news: Germany holds national day of remembrance

Events were held for "Volkstrauertag," a day commemorating victims of war and oppression. Meanwhile, experts said the country is headed for a budget crisis.

This live blog is now closed. Read on for a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of November 14-15, 2026:

Thank you for reading this weekend's Germany news blog.

We'll bring you more from the heart of Europe on Monday. We wish you a very Schönen Abend!

Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen has urged Europeans to defend compassion and humanity during Germany's national day of mourning for victims of war and oppression.

Speaking at a ceremony in the Bundestag in Berlin, Van der Bellen warned against becoming desensitized to suffering despite the constant images of war and violence.

"Compassion is not a weakness; it is a human strength; it is the foundation of humanity," he said.

He also addressed the responsibility of later generations for the crimes of the past.

Although people today bore no personal guilt for their ancestors' actions, he said, they were responsible for what they learned from history and how they treated others.

"Let us ensure that our home, Europe, remains a place where people can live in peace, freedom and dignity," he said.

Bundestag President Julia Klöckner also called for the defense of democracy, pointing to Ukrainians risking their lives to protect freedom.

Germany's Volkstrauertag commemorates soldiers and civilians killed in war, as well as victims of Nazi persecution and other forms of oppression.

German police have arrested three suspects after thieves rammed a car into a jewelry store in the Bavarian city of Bayreuth and stole valuables worth around €10,000 ($11,600).

Bavarian Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann said the stolen items included jewelry and silver coins.

The burglars drove a car into the store early in the morning before fleeing in a second vehicle, police said.

Officers spotted the getaway car on the A9 highway and gave chase. The suspects left the highway near Weidensees, abandoned their vehicle beside a wooded area and fled on foot.

Police launched a search involving patrol cars, dogs, drones and a helicopter.

All three suspects were subsequently arrested, with some of the stolen goods recovered.

Prosecutors are expected to decide whether to seek pretrial detention for the suspects.

Detroit Lions receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown played his first NFL American football game in Germany in Munich.

St. Brown made his professional debut in Germany as the Detroit Lions faced the New England Patriots at Munich's Allianz Arena. The 27-year-old grew up in Southern California, and his mother, Miriam, is from Leverkusen. Both his parents were due to watch from the stands.

The NFL player spent childhood summers with his grandparents in the Rhineland.

"This is awesome. A dream come true," St. Brown said before the game. Asked by German broadcaster RTL what he had been looking forward to most, he reeled off a list that included schnitzel, potato dumplings, sauerkraut, currywurst and fries with mayonnaise.

"I'm really excited. I can't wait," he said. "Being in Germany with my teammates and my family — I want to enjoy it and take it all in."

Two people were slightly injured after an unidentified man threw a firework into the entrance of a gay bar in Frankfurt, police said.

The attack took place at the Zum Schwejk bar, a venue popular with the city's gay community, on Saturday evening.

Police said the bar was clearly identifiable as an LGBTQ+ venue because of a rainbow flag displayed outside.

The motive remains unclear, and police have not said whether they suspect a homophobic attack.

Officers are investigating suspected aggravated assault and have appealed for witnesses.

The bar said it was "shocked and stunned" by the incident and apologized to guests who witnessed it. It said it wanted to be a place where everyone felt welcome, respected and safe, and pledged to do everything it could to prevent a repeat.

Andreas Ewald, LGBTQ+ policy spokesperson for the Greens in the Hesse state parliament, condemned the attack and called for those responsible to face the full force of the law.

He also urged the state government to establish a roundtable on LGBTQ+ safety involving community representatives, police and victim support organizations.

The bar's name refers to a Czech soldier in the satirical anti-war novel "The Good Soldier Svejk."

Police in Berlin have filed 28 criminal charges against demonstrators who marched throught the capital on Saturday as part of the Gen Z regelt (Gen Z Takes Charge) movement.

Some 1,200 demonstrators took part in the march, although only 100 had registered for the event under German laws regulating public protests.

The protesters complained about dilapidated schools, the threat of compulsory military service, cuts to university and social funding and other issues.

Police said there had been some clashes with participants.   A police spokeswoman said the criminal charges were filed for riot, assault, resisting officers and violations of explosives regulations.

Three police officers of the 700 deployed to ensure securty were injured during the demonstration.

November 20 is likely to see more large protests in both Germany and Europe, with some 15,000 demonstrators registered for a march in Berlin.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has expressed solidarity with the Jewish community in Germany amid what he described as ever "louder and more aggressive" antisemitic voices.

Speaking at the presentation of the Prize for Understanding and Tolerance awarded by the Jewish Museum in Berlin, Steinmeier said: "For all those to whom our country, its constitution and the values it enshrines mean something, there can be only one answer to such antisemitism: to stand side by side with Jewish people in our country."

Steinmeier said he deplored the frequent vandalism of memorials to Nazi crimes.

"I am profoundly ashamed of that all," he said, saying that anyone who mocked the work of museums and memorial sites or collectively blamed, threatened and attacked Jews "attacks the heart of our republic."

The president also congratulated the prize winners — German journalist and author Düzen Tekkal and British philanthropist Michael Moritz — on their awards.

In a citation, the museum described Tekkal as a champion of human rights who consistently opposed antisemitism and racism while promoting interfaith dialogue, equality in education and opportunities, peace and democracy.

The museum commended Moritz for supporting artistic projects that show Jewish perspectives and strengthen social dialogue.

The Jewish Museum, which is marking its 25th anniversary this year, has been presenting the prize since 2002.

Some 600 sheep have made their way through the southern city of Nuremberg on their way to western winter pasturage, watched by crowds of spectators.

The sheep follow an around 10-km-long (6-mile-long) route that crosses a number of streets and the market square.

The annual event is meant, among other things, to draw attention to the tradition of transhumant, or itinerant, sheep-keeping in the region and the benefits the animals have for landscape conservation.

"With their grazing in summer, sheep create great biodiversity in many important biotopes in the urban region," the city of Nuremberg said ahead of the migration.

Thieves have stolen several valuable items from a jewelry shop in the southern city of Bayreuth after ramming it with a car, police said on Sunday.

They said a black Mercedes carrying three people crashed into the shop in the early hours of Sunday morning.

The burglars then fled the scene in a second Mercedes, this time a gray one, after taking a number of articles.

The getaway car was then spotted by a police patrol on a motorway heading south, with officers setting off in pursuit.

The suspects were then said to have driven off the motorway to a patch of woodland where they abandoned their vehicle and went on by foot.

Police searched for the fugitives with patrol cars, police dogs, drones and a helicopter, a statement said.

Two men were reportedly arrested with a third still on the run. Investigators are looking into whether the detainees were connected with the theft.

Events are taking place around Germany for the Volkstrauertag (people's day of mourning), a day on which armed forces personnel and civilians who died in armed conflicts and victims of violent state oppression are commemorated.

Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen is to speak in the parliament at the main commemoration ceremony of the German War Graves Commission at midday.

His presence reflects the large number of Austrians who were killed in action in the Second World War while fighting for the German Wehrmacht following the annexation of their country by Nazi Germany in 1938.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the patron of the commission, will also hold a speech and lay a wreath.

Last year, Steinmeier decreed that the Volkstrauertag should also commemorate people who were persecuted and killed by the Nazis because of their sexual identity, as well as police officers who have lost their lives in the course of duty.

There will also be a remembrance ceremony at the Jewish Cemetery in Berlin for those of the Jewish faith killed in World War I.

In remarks to the DPA news agency ahead of the remembrance day, the speaker of the lower house of German parliament, or Bundestag, Julia Klöckner, called on society to actively defend democracy.

Klöckner said that the Volkstrauertag was a reminder of how destructive tyranny and contempt for human dignity can be.

"Democracy is the antidote here," she said. "But it is not an heirloom. It wastes away when we do not constantly renew its promise of basic rights and freedom."

Guten Morgen from the DW newsroom on the banks of the Rhine in Bonn!

You join us as Germany holds a day of remembrance for the victims of war and oppression and also commemorates members of the police force killed while carrying out their duties.

Read on here for the top stories from and about Germany on Sunday, November 15,

It's 1 a.m. here and time for us to pause our coverage of news from Germany.

We'll be back Sunday morning with more of what's making headlines in Berlin, Bavaria and the rest of the country.

Germany wants to turn its spies into "real secret agents." A sweeping reform could allow them to sabotage threats abroad and use AI to analyze intelligence data.

But why does Germany need these powers now? And how far can its secret services go in a country with a history of strict limits on intelligence operations?

Hundreds of mourners gathered at Munich's Frauenkirche on Saturday to pay their final respects to Hubert Aiwanger, Bavaria's former deputy premier and economy minister, who died unexpectedly at the age of 55.

The ceremony combined a Catholic funeral Mass with a state memorial service, attended by leading political figures, church representatives and members of Bavaria's former royal family.

Bavarian Premier Markus Söder recalled his disbelief when he first heard of Aiwanger's death in a Berlin hotel on November 4. He described his former deputy as someone who had always been full of energy.

Bavarian parliament president Ilse Aigner praised Aiwanger as one of the greatest political talents of his generation, highlighting his role in transforming his party "Freie Wähler" (Free Voters) from a local political movement into a governing party.

Aiwanger's partner, Tanja Schweiger, and their two sons were among those attending the service, which took place eleven days after his death.

German airline group Lufthansa says it was only slightly affected by Friday's temporary suspension of flights to the United States.

Most flights operated as scheduled, although some were canceled or delayed. Lufthansa expects its US flight schedule to return to normal on Saturday but warned that isolated delays could still occur.

Affected passengers are being notified by email, with alternative travel options provided automatically in the event of cancellations.

The disruption was caused by problems with the US air traffic control system. Domestic flights in the US were grounded for around four hours, marking the longest nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks in 2001.

#630. NASA is offering $1 million for bold ideas to help build a Moon base

NASA has launched a $1 million Moon Base Challenge, inviting teams of students from high schools and colleges across the United States to help develop ideas for humanity's future on the Moon. The competition was announced during a MAX POWER event at Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida. Presented as part of a Golden Age of Science, the initiative gives young innovators an opportunity to contribute designs and potential solutions for NASA's planned lunar base.

"We're looking for students ready to think creatively, work as a team, and take on real problems connected to NASA's future on the Moon," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. "You do not have to wait until graduation to contribute. Curiosity, creativity, and the willingness to tackle hard problems without obvious answers are exactly the qualities we need as we build what comes next."

NASA is working toward establishing a Moon Base near the lunar South Pole, where astronauts will be able to live, conduct research, and explore the surrounding region. Creating a lasting human presence on the Moon is also an important step toward future missions that will carry astronauts to Mars. Achieving these goals will require expertise and creative thinking from people across a wide range of industries and disciplines.

"As we build and design the foundations of Moon Base, we want to leverage all the ingenuity and innovation to think of every consideration our explorers might need to live and work there," said Carlos García-Galán, manager, Moon Base Program. "Students bring exactly the bold ideas that we're looking for, and I'm looking forward to their fresh perspective. Ultimately, Moon Base is for them, people who will experience a world where humans are on the Moon to stay."

Six Major Challenges of Living on the Moon

The competition will unfold in multiple phases, with student teams developing solutions to six essential aspects of operating a lunar base. These include generating and storing power, constructing facilities, maintaining life support systems, enabling transportation across the lunar surface, establishing communications networks, and protecting astronauts.

Each category addresses practical obstacles that NASA must overcome to support long-term operations on the Moon. By working on these problems, students can explore new approaches to lunar technologies while developing technical and professional skills that could prepare them for careers in aerospace and related fields.

The challenge is designed around actual environmental conditions and mission requirements that would affect daily life and operations on the lunar surface. Participants will produce work similar to that used in the space industry, including evaluations of competing technical options, proposals outlining potential designs, and presentations for project stakeholders.

Students from technical, vocational, and other academic backgrounds are encouraged to participate. Previous specialized knowledge of engineering or related technical fields is not required, making the competition accessible to a broad range of young innovators.

Inspiring the Next Generation of Space Explorers

Beyond generating ideas for the Moon Base, NASA hopes the competition will help develop the skills needed by the next generation of aerospace professionals. By exposing students to practical design challenges, the agency aims to encourage collaboration, creative problem-solving, and greater involvement in future space exploration.

"Students are the next generation of explorers and innovators. Their unique perspectives are key to helping us envision a future away from Earth, and I'm excited to see the creativity and ingenuity spurred by this challenge," said Elaine Ho, associate administrator for the Office of STEM Engagement at NASA Headquarters.

How to Enter NASA's $1 Million Moon Base Challenge

Interested student teams must register through the NASA STEM Gateway. Registration remains open until January 25, 2027.

NASA's Office of STEM Engagement developed the competition in partnership with the agency's Moon Base Program. The Institute of Competition Sciences is responsible for administering the challenge under a contract with NASA's Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation, which operates within the Research and Technology Mission Directorate.

#629. Despite restrictive abortion laws, Poland's 'Abortomat' — a locker that dispenses abortion pills — helps women who want to end a pregnancy

Abortion laws in Poland are very restrictive. Activists there have found a new way to help women wanting to terminate a pregnancy: the "Abortomat," a locker that dispenses abortion pills. But they face fierce opposition.

Women's rights activists in Poland have opened what they say is the world's first delivery locker supplying abortion pills in a country with one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws.

Known as the "Abortomat," the locker is in a building opposite the Polish parliament, in what activists say is a clear message to politicians like Donald Tusk. The Polish prime minister pledged to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy before the 2023 parliamentary election, but his coalition has been unable to agree on a common position.

Only two European Union member states, Poland and Malta, do not allow abortion on request.

In Poland, abortion is only allowed when the pregnancy is the result of a crime — rape or incest — or when it endangers the health or life of the woman.

Justyna Wydrzynska, an activist from a nonprofit organization called Abortion Dream Team, showed DW the "Abortomat" in a small room behind a tasseled portiere at Abotak, Poland's first abortion center.

Inside, the pink lighting is subdued. Glitter tassels, baubles and spotlights make it feel a bit like a disco, she said.

The "Abortomat," which opened in late September, has 22 pink lockers. To open one, a woman receives a PIN code from the organization Women Help Women after completing a medical questionnaire, which is then checked by a doctor.

Parcel lockers have sprung up like mushrooms after rain in Poland in recent years. Even the smallest villages have them.

"When you walk around Poland, vending machines are everywhere. This is our culture. People in the US have Amazon, we have vending machines for everything," said Wydrzynska.

Women in Poland who have an abortion are not criminalized. But anyone who helps them terminate a pregnancy risks up to three years in prison.

In 2023, Wydrzynska was the first activist to be convicted in Poland of helping a woman to have an abortion by sending her pills. The conviction was later overturned, and the court ordered a retrial.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Inside each compartment at the "Abortomat" is a package that normally contains two drugs, mifepristone and misoprostol, usually taken up to the 14th week of pregnancy.

Because mifepristone is not registered in Poland, the drug must be ordered from abroad where it is legal. Information on how to do this is not easy to come by, which is where Abortion Dream Team and Abotak come in. They help women find information about accessing medication, which is sent from abroad by Women Help Women, or help them to travel abroad for a termination.

Wydrzynska said she believes the "Abortomat" does not break the law because it is a machine, not a person, that is delivering the pills, although she admits she is not sure.

Dr. Sabrina Mana-Walasek, a reproductive rights lawyer representing Wydrzynska, said the legal environment for abortion pills is "complicated."

She said that although mifepristone is not registered in Poland, it is registered in the European Union and, as EU citizens, Polish women can order it and take it.

"If a woman orders pills for herself and pays for them herself, it's not a crime," she said.

The ultra-Catholic legal group Ordo Iuris disagrees and has notified the prosecutor's office that the activists are committing a crime.

"In the case of an 'Abortomat,' the actions enabling a woman to have an abortion are theoretically performed by the woman herself using the device, but the reality is that this machine is operated by people — they send the code required to open the compartment containing abortion pills, they order and procure the pills, and they restock the compartments," said Katarzyna Gesiak, director of the Ordo Iuris Center for Medical Law and Bioethics.

Wydrzynska said anti-abortion activists regularly demonstrate outside Abotak, using horns and loudspeakers to generate loud noise to annoy the center's residential neighbors and pressure the landlord to revoke their rental agreement.

At one demonstration, a woman holding an image of the Virgin Mary told DW she believes abortion "is the work of Satan."

"Abortion is evil, it's demonic, it's against the fifth Commandment, 'Thou shalt not kill,'" she said.

Earlier this year, Diana, a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman living in Warsaw, used abortion pills during her sixth week of pregnancy before the "Abortomat" started up. She got the pills using information provided by Abortion Dream Team.

Diana told DW that she has never wanted to have children.

"I was expecting something like a headache, stomachache, maybe vomiting, but I had nothing like that. It was just like a normal period. I didn't feel any pain. It was really easy for me," she said.

"I felt relief because I knew that it was the right choice for me. I knew that I can live my life," she added.

Another Abortion Dream Team activist, Natalia Broniarczyk, said they help about 130 women daily in Poland. About 125 of these women use pills that cost about €75 ($83), while the remainder travel to a clinic abroad.

In contrast, just 851 abortions were performed in Polish hospitals last year.

Broniarczyk is concerned about the rising support for right-wing parties ahead of next year's parliamentary election, but she's also furious at the inactivity of liberals in Tusk's coalition.

"I'm mad at the liberals because for three years, they did nothing to protect us. They lost three years and now, when we're close to an election, they are fighting for our voices and respect. People are more progressive than politicians," she said.

After taking office in 2023, Tusk's coalition, which includes left-wing and conservative partners, were unable to agree a common position and their separate bills failed to obtain parliamentary approval in 2024.

Afterwards, Tusk said abortion on request would not be possible during the current parliamentary term.

In October, however, two bills were resubmitted to the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, and were narrowly approved.

One reinstates severe irreversible fetal defects as a justification for a legal termination. This justification had been ruled illegal by the Constitutional Court in 2020 when the previous right-wing Law and Justice (PiS)-led government was in power.

The 2020 ruling led to tens of thousands of people, mostly women, taking part in street protests in towns and cities across the country, some of the largest since communism fell in 1989.

Lawmakers also approved a bill partially decriminalizing anyone who helps a woman terminate her pregnancy.

According to the results of a recent poll conducted by SW Research for Onet.pl, almost 61% of respondents said they want the country's right-wing president, Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, to sign into law the bill on the fetal defect justification.

Nawrocki opposes abortion, and both Wydrzynska and Broniarczyk think he will use his power of veto to block the bills, preventing them from becoming law.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

STARBASE, Texas  — I just finished covering the Starship Flight 15 mission, and SpaceXs incredible launch tower catch of the returned Ship 42 spacecraft isn't the only thing over the weekend that left me speechless.

The morning of the launch (Nov. 13), SpaceX invited media on a tour of Starbase's Starfactory facility, where it manufactures and assembles both stages of its massive Starship rocket - an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the production and scale of SpaceX's operations, and a glimpse of things to come as Starship notches more and more milestones the more it flies.

For some context, the five-story-tall Starfactory spans approximately 1 million square feet (~93,000 meters), with operations split between Starship's Super Heavy boosters and upper stage Ships, and nearly 330,000 additional square feet (30,000 square meters) of office space. SpaceX officials describe its design as one more akin to an automotive manufacturing plant than that of a typical aerospace production site, and inside, it is absolutely alive with activity.

We entered through an arch-covered doorway underneath the giant "X" sign on the building's shorter face. Our media gaggle was met with curious glances as we were shown through the doors and guided onto the factory floor - few are ever able to cross that threshold outside of SpaceX employees, and our presence seemed as novel to those busy working as it was to us.

Inside, we were struck with the sheer enormity of Starship's scale. Giant stainless-steel rocket parts were meticulously scattered across different subassembly stations throughout the building, with Ship nose cones, cylindrical sections and booster components all under various stages of manufacture. The sheer quantity of the hardware was staggering, and being so close to each as we walked Starfactory's throughways was an eye-opener.

Starbase is a unique partnership of privately-owned SpaceX property and publicly-accessible land and shoreline, which has created the unique ability for anyone with a mind to do so to drive right up to the the Starship launch pad to see the facilities up close (within a few hundred feet or so, which, as rockets go, is very, very close).

Fully stacked, Starship stands more than 400 feet (120 meters) tall. Standing next to such a towering colossus on the pad is enough to drive home just how big the launch vehicle is, but standing next its segmented components inside Starfactory is even more humbling; like seeing one of Ship's upper aerodynamic flaps, which are each large enough when laid flat that you could park a pair of large SUVs on their faces with room to spare.

Starbase, Texas https://t.co/NqDWwUZXv9August 25, 2025

As our tour continued and we passed rows of nose cones under preparation for integration, numbering as high as Ship 51, one stood out from the others. In the distance, only visible for moment between the overlapping views of other Ships as we walked through the production stations, was a nose cone with a series of windows cut out of its face - undoubtedly a prototype for, or possibly even the final article that will be used as NASA's Artemis lunar lander.

NASA has contracted SpaceX to develop a version of Starship capable of landing astronauts on the moon as a part of the agency's Artemis program, and this appeared to the Ship being readied for when that mission arrives. NASA is targeting Artemis IV as the program's first crewed lunar landing in 2028, and while the decision solidifying Starship as the lander tasked with that mission isn't finalized (Blue Origin is also vying for that spot with its Blue Moon lander), SpaceX is clearly operating with the intention of coming out ahead.

But Artemis is clearly not SpaceX's only focus, as evident by the many, many other Ships in production that did not have window holes carved out of them.SpaceX officials said the company is currently completing about one Ship upper stage every two weeks, and one Super Heavy booster every four weeks, with overlapping production allowing multiple rockets to move through the factory simultaneously. The majority of the vehicles currently being assembled will carry stacks of SpaceX's upgraded Starlink Version 3 (V3) satellites.

The company's Starlink network in low Earth orbit currently consists of more than 11,000 spacecraft beaming wireless internet to SpaceX customers across the globe. All of those were launched on SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9 rocket, with the exception of a few more than 50 delivered on Starship's two most recent test flights. Both carried V3 Starlink stacks to add to the constellation, which SpaceX officials say each added the data capacity equivalent to ten Falcon 9 Starlink launches. And, as they fine tune Starship's design, SpaceX plans to increase the vehicle's launch cadence dramatically, growing the Starlink network as it does.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has stated the company hopes to launch Starship about once a week beginning in 2027, and with the number of Ships we saw lined up inside Starfactory, launch vehicle inventory doesn't seem like it will be to blame if that goal isn't realized.

SpaceX has adopted a manufacturing process modeled after the automotive industry, where efficiency and reproduction allow for the manufacture of large numbers of identical parts. Automation is a critical part of that process, but not one SpaceX is ready to entirely rely on.

Much of the equipment and tools being used for Starship's production were designed by SpaceX engineers, who are constantly refining production processes to eliminate bottlenecks. And SpaceX has deliberately kept technicians on the floor as Starship's design continues to evolve, rather than automating procedures that might soon become obsolete.

Our tour guide compared SpaceX's manufacturing consistency goals to that of Lego bricks, which are famously precise in their production down to the micro-millimeter accuracy of what now number more than 1 trillion bricks made since the toy company began in the 1940s.

Exiting the far side of the building, we stood in the shadow of SpaceX's two towering Mega Bays, where the sections of Starship are stacked and integrated with their engines - there's one hanger for Ship, and another for Super Heavy. Each can hold about five or six assemblies, and housed two or three vehicles at the time our tour was brought by.

Both Mega Bays, however, looked small against the adjacent Gigabay SpaceX is currently constructing. At approximately 700,000 square feet (65,000 square meters), Gigabay will be equipped with room to accommodate up to 24 vehicles at a time, and will facilitate a major increase in SpaceX's ability to assemble its Ship and Super Heavy rockets.

Part of SpaceX's goal with Starship is to make all of what we got to see completely routine; to make rocket launches and landings as ordinary as commercial airline flights. Still, standing inside Starfactory, surrounded on all sides by huge spacecraft in various stages of assembly, it was hard to imagine a reality where giant rockets flying to and from space on a regular basis wouldn't feel like science fiction.

Later that day a giant rocket launched to outer space - Super Heavy did attempt a return to pad, but was diverted for an offshore landing instead, where it exploded. But the next day, Ship 42 came plunging through the overcast cloud cover, falling belly-first toward the same tower it left just a couple dozen hours before. And then it lit its engines and was caught by the tower.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

#627. ESA’s Hera spacecraft is flying rectangles around NASA’s asteroid crash site

The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has reached its destination, arriving near two asteroids that could help scientists learn how to protect Earth from dangerous space rocks. The spacecraft, which is roughly the size of a small car, is now traveling about 25 to 30 kilometers from the Didymos asteroid system as it begins its first scientific observations.

This initial stage, known as the "early characterization phase," is designed to give researchers a broad understanding of the two asteroids and their surroundings. Of particular interest is Dimorphos, the smaller asteroid that NASA deliberately struck with its DART spacecraft in 2022 to test whether a collision could change an asteroid's path.

"Our aim right now is to gather the big-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission's planetary defense goals," explains mission scientist Michael Kueppers.

"During this phase, our images will reveal for the first time what a small asteroid looks like globally, having experienced a hypervelocity impact in the context of the first asteroid deflection test, when NASA's DART spacecraft impacted it to change its orbit in 2022."

"Previous predictions by our impact models suggested many different ways the asteroid body might react, but Hera will reveal which forecast was the correct one - if any!"

Why Hera Is Flying in Rectangles Around Two Asteroids

Navigating around asteroids presents challenges that are very different from those encountered by spacecraft exploring planets. The main asteroid, Didymos, measures approximately 780 meters across and has gravitational pull about 40,000 times weaker than Earth's. Its smaller companion, Dimorphos, is just 151 meters wide and has gravity roughly 200,000 times weaker than Earth's.

With gravity this weak, maintaining a conventional circular orbit is not practical. Hera instead travels around the shared center of gravity of the two asteroids, moving at a remarkably slow speed of approximately 12 centimeters per second. That is comparable to the pace of an insect crawling quickly across the ground.

Rather than following a smooth circular path, Hera moves along nearly straight trajectories. At alternating intervals of three and four days, the spacecraft fires its thrusters while moving away from the asteroids, changing direction by 90 degrees. These carefully timed maneuvers create a series of unusual "rectangular orbits" that keep Hera approximately 25 to 30 kilometers from the asteroid pair.

The unusual navigation strategy builds on experience gained during ESA's Rosetta comet mission. It also provides an important safety advantage. If a planned thruster firing fails, Hera will naturally drift farther from the asteroids instead of moving toward a potentially dangerous collision. Because the spacecraft travels so slowly, each course correction requires very little propellant.

Hera Prepares for a Closer Look at the Asteroids

Next month, Hera is expected to begin its "detailed characterization phase," bringing it significantly closer to Didymos and Dimorphos. During this stage, the spacecraft will switch from rectangular flight paths to more complex hyperbolic trajectories shaped like bowties, beginning at distances of approximately 20 kilometers.

The mission is directed from ESA's ESOC mission control center in Darmstadt, Germany. Despite Hera being approximately 196.5 million kilometers from Earth, controllers maintain contact with the spacecraft for about eight hours each day.

Communication is handled through four enormous Deep Space Antennas, each measuring 35 meters in diameter, at facilities in Argentina, Spain, and Australia.

The mission control team also works closely with ESA's Flight Dynamics team. Using data transmitted by Hera, these specialists calculate its exact location relative to the two asteroids and develop the commands needed to guide it safely from one planned position to another.

Investigating NASA's Historic Asteroid Collision

Hera's observations will help answer some of the biggest questions left unanswered by NASA's first asteroid deflection experiment.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately collided with Dimorphos. The 580-kilogram spacecraft struck the asteroid at approximately 6.1 kilometers per second, producing a massive cloud of debris that spread across 10,000 kilometers of space.

The impact successfully changed Dimorphos' motion, shortening the time it takes to orbit Didymos by about 33 minutes. This was a major achievement for planetary defense, demonstrating that deliberately crashing a spacecraft into an asteroid could alter its trajectory.

However, the experiment also raised important questions. Scientists still do not know exactly how the impact changed Dimorphos itself. Did the collision excavate a large crater, or did it significantly reshape the entire asteroid?

Researchers also need more precise information about Dimorphos' composition, internal structure, and mass. Understanding these properties could explain why the impact produced a much larger orbital change than computer simulations had predicted.

These details are essential for developing the collision method, known as kinetic impact, into a dependable planetary defense strategy. If scientists can determine how different types of asteroids respond to being struck, they will be better equipped to predict the results of future attempts to redirect potentially hazardous objects.

A Close-Up Investigation of the Asteroid Crash Site

Over the coming months, Hera will conduct a detailed investigation of Dimorphos, effectively examining the scene of NASA's historic collision.

The spacecraft will use several scientific instruments to study the asteroid and will release two small CubeSats, each about the size of a shoebox. These miniature spacecraft will travel even closer to the asteroid to collect additional measurements, with the mission eventually advancing to landing operations.

Together, the observations should provide scientists with a much clearer understanding of how Dimorphos responded to DART's impact and why the experiment worked so effectively. That knowledge could prove crucial if Earth ever faces a dangerous asteroid on a collision course.

The Himalayas tower below the clouds, capped in icy snow in new snapshots captured from aboard the International Space Station.

Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk was looking out one of the windows aboard the space station when the most incredible view came into focus  — and thankfully he had a camera handy and was able to capture these striking scenes of the Himalayas from space.

Above the mountain range, fluffy clouds hang in the atmosphere. Below, the expansive Himalayas are covered in bright snow and ice, which looks somehow both white and blue at the same time as the bright sunlight streaks across the breathtaking expanse.

This frosty winter scene showcases the mountain range from orbit, from about 250 miles (400 kilometers) above Earth's surface. But even from this distance, the magnitude of this mountain range is palpable. The Himalayas stretch across five different countries including Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan. And the Himalayas include some of the highest mountain peaks on planet Earth, including Mount Everest.

Himalayas 🗻 https://t.co/IzGzu20H4QNovember 17, 2026

From orbit around Earth, you might expect even the largest landmarks on our planet to appear miniscule. But somehow, in these photographs snapped by Kutryk during NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission, even from hundreds of miles above our planet you can really see and feel the immense scale of this mammoth mountain range.

It's unclear exactly where above the mountain range these photographs were taken, but it is always amazing to think that within these sweeping landscapes are people living their lives, likely unaware that an astronaut is taking in the beauty of their home.

Perhaps somewhere hidden under the clouds in one of Kutryk's photographs are hikers climbing up the side of Mt. Everest, completing their own bucket list adventure as the astronauts watching from above complete theirs.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. #625. Dig review: Amy Poehler and Parks and Recs Mike Schur have done it again

The first time Amy Poehler and Mike Schur teamed up for a series about Poehler rolling up her sleeves and getting to work in a massive dirt pit, they gave us Parks and Recreation, a charming workplace sitcom about the power of friendship and doing what you love. The second time Amy Poehler and Mike Schur teamed up for a series about Poehler rolling up her sleeves and getting to work in a massive dirt pit, they gave us Peacock's new series Dig, which is — you guessed it! — a charming workplace sitcom about the power of friendship and doing what you love.

Story-wise, the two shows are miles apart. Literally. The former takes place in the decidedly unglamorous town of Pawnee, Indiana, while the latter, based on Kate Myers' novel Excavations, transports us to a sun-bleached archaeological dig in Greece. Yet despite the flashy location and a new mystery twist, Dig retains the core formula that made Parks and Recreation so irresistible: investing deeply in a lovable new crew of unlikely friends.

Kicking off that group is Elise (Poehler), the lead archaeologist on a long-running dig in southern Greece. She's qualified and passionate, yet has a hard time connecting with the undergraduates (or UGs) participating in the dig. Because of her more guarded exterior, she's consistently second fiddle to longtime dig leader Neville (Hugh Laurie). Perpetually on the brink of retirement, Neville seems unable to cede control of the dig to Elise, both because of his love for archaeology and the ego boost his role gives him. He's the Lucy to Elise's Charlie Brown, constantly yanking the football away at the last second.

So, when Elise discovers a perfectly preserved statue of Hera at an older dig site, the last thing she wants to do is tell Neville and give him an opportunity to claim any shred of credit. However, hiding any cultural artifacts from Neville and the Grecian government at large is illegal, so Elise must assemble a crack team to help her cover up her covert dig of the Hera statue, whom they nickname "Pretty Woman." First up is Dylan (Geraldine Viswanathan), an always flaky wild card who has unfinished business at the dig. Joining her are Clare (Antonia Thomas), a prim and proper conservator born with a silver spoon in her mouth, and Patty (Fina Strazza), a sheltered farm girl with a deep passion for Greek mythology.

Like with most sitcoms, the characters begin as the broadest versions of themselves before revealing their deeper nuances. At first, Elise is prickly to a fault, allowing Poehler to sidestep any preconceived comparisons you might want to draw to Leslie Knope. Elsewhere, Dylan is the hottest of hot messes, Clare is a haughty queen bee, and Patty is an out-of-her-depth klutz. They border on parodies instead of full-bodied characters, making Dig's earlier episodes a bit lukewarm.

But as Dig's title suggests, this is a show that won't be satisfied by sticking at surface level. As the show delves into what makes its characters tick, it becomes a heartwarming tale of found family, not unlike many other beloved Schur shows. Suddenly, character traits that felt one-note to start are revealed to be defense mechanisms or misconceptions, adding entirely new dimensions to Dig's core four.

Dig works best when that core works together in earnest, which is another reason why the show's early entries feel like slower burns: They're doing the groundwork to loop every woman into the Pretty Woman dig. Once they're all on the same page, Dig gets off and running — even more so once Pretty Woman mysteriously vanishes, leaving Elise and her motley crew to do some boots-on-the-ground detective work. Thus begins a madcap caper involving stakeouts, undercover identities, and the black market.

Along the way, Elise, Dylan, Clare, and Patty are allowed to be wonderfully messy and vulnerable, all while staying refreshingly supportive of one another. For example, a love triangle burbles up between Clare, Dylan, and Clare's fiancé/Dylan's ex-boyfriend Gary (Jon Pointing), yet the storyline never devolves into cat fights or possessiveness. Instead, Dig focuses more on what these relationships mean to Clare and Dylan beyond romance. For Clare, her engagement is a sign of stability and true adulthood, whereas Dylan is looking for closure, something she notoriously can never get.

Dig also dabbles in intergenerational conflict, highlighting the differences between each of its leads, all of whom are at very different stages in their lives. Again, Dig doesn't take a hackneyed "Gen Z versus millennials versus Gen X" route. It's more interested in showing the different wants that motivate us. Patty yearns for belonging and friendship, while Elise wants to cement her legacy and make sure she's done something big enough to call her own, no Neville required.

Once Dig's ensemble truly comes together, they mesh wonderfully. Poehler brings a weary exasperation to Elise that slowly gives way to warm leadership, a transformation that's a joy to witness. Thomas and Viswanathan are perfect foils, the former a picture of poise, the latter completely uninhibited. Watching them feed off each other offers up a perfect comedic contrast. Finally, there's Strazza, whose endearingly goofy Patty becomes the beating heart of the show. Laurie, too, is a joy, blending Neville's smarminess with a genial charm that makes him infuriatingly tough to hate.

In focusing on archaeology, Dig emphasizes the importance of excavating ancient objects and interrogating the stories of those who once used them. In many ways, Dig is doing the same thing with its characters: peeling back their layers to get at their core truths. Only instead of using trowels and brushes, Dig uses the power of the workplace sitcom. It's a power Schur and his collaborators know well, and the result is a show that will leave you feeling like you've just uncovered something great in a dig of your own — with far less dirt on your face and clothes, that is.

#624. German economy returns to growth, so why is the country still worried?

The German economy is growing again, albeit slightly. However, economists warn that without reforms, higher productivity and solid public finances, a loss of prosperity and growing debt threaten future generations.

Is Germany's economy back on the up? The answer to that question depends on your perspective.

At the 2026 Mechanical Engineering Summit in Berlin this week, the mood was sullen. "A year ago, I said here: We are angry. Today I must say: We are stunned," Bertram Kawlath, president of the Mechanical Engineering Industry Association (VDMA), said in his opening remarks on Tuesday.

The mechanical and plant engineering sector was the backbone of German industry for decades. It once employed more than a million people; now 15,000 positions are being cut every month. Production has shrunk about 20% since 2018.

Kawlath criticized the federal government's infighting and lack of reform, as well as what the companies consider a continued high bureaucracy and tax burden.

"[We are] stunned by the whitewashing in so many government statements. Stunned by the increasingly visible decline of our country as a business location."

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz promised quick reforms and a rapidly noticeable economic upswing when he took office in May 2025. A year and a half later, reality has caught up with him.

Merz's coalition of his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), its Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union, (CSU), along with the center-left Social Democrats(SPD), keeps running into trouble. In addition, there are crises and wars. The German economy is facing more headwinds than seldom before, Merz said in October at the German Employers' Day conference in Berlin.

Given the circumstances, small successes are even more meaningful. "A heartfelt thanks for the good news you bring," Merz said when he received the autumn report of the Council of Economic Experts in Berlin, which predicted economic growth of 1.3% for 2026 and 1% for 2027.

The economic experts have a German government mandate to independently analyze business activity and make recommendations for economic policy. Earlier this year, they were much more pessimistic.

"The German economy has recovered quicker than expected from the energy price shock sparked by the war in Iran," said Monika Schnitzer, chair of the expert advisory board, explaining the prognosis. "We see a significant economic recovery, driven by surprisingly strong exports and high government spending."

The chancellor, who celebrated his 71st birthday on November 11, spoke of "encouraging signals" in his address. "The economy in Germany is slowly on the rise again. Considering the many crises in Germany, it was not totally expected that we would manage that."

But these improved prospects do not change the long-term problems. An ageing society means the bills for pensions, health and caregiving are constantly rising.

At the same time, the number of working-age people who finance these services is sinking. That puts increasing pressure on the public purse. According to Berlin's financial planning, social welfare costs, defense and interest on debt will account for 80% of the spending in the federal government's budget.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"We must realize that in the long term the expected revenues in the federal budget will not be enough to cover the planned expenses," Schnitzer warned. The growth rates are far below what is needed to secure the same level of prosperity as previous decades in the long term.

"To grow out of this budgetary predicament, we would need levels of economic growth which we haven't experienced in Germany for the past 50 years," she said.

The government is currently in final deliberations over its 2027 budget; spending upwards of €555 billion ($615 billion) is planned. Because revenue won't be enough to cover it, the government is planning to take on more than €118 billion in new debt. Adding the debt-financed special funds for infrastructure and the military, the new borrowing adds up to almost €204 billion.

The economic experts have warned that if Germany continues with this path, the debt-to-GDP ratio could rise to 100% by 2040. This ratio indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output. At the end of 2025, it was 63.5%.

Germany is the only country of the world's leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) to still hold a AAA rating, the best possible credit rating in finance markets. It signals to investors the smallest possible default risk for German government bonds. "I want it to stay that way," Merz emphasized.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, taking on less debt will not be simple. "A reduction in debt-based financing presents policymakers with a consolidation task of historic proportions and will require tough decisions," said Schnitzer. The belt-tightening must, however, be designed to enable growth. Some recommendations include reducing environmentally harmful tax benefits — like the energy tax breaks for diesel fuel.

The so-called "mothers' pension", a pension subsidy for older parents, should be revoked, said the experts. Tax increases could become necessary in the medium term, for example with value-added tax.

"The burden should be shared fairly between generations and societal groups," Schnitzer said.

According to the chancellor, the experts' message has been received. Solid state finances are an issue in Germany but also throughout the European Union. Merz said there needs to be a consolidation course, adding that politicians have a duty to the younger generation. Reforms are needed, especially when it comes to social security systems.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Economic researchers are setting their hopes on increasing companies' productivity. Put simply, productivity describes how much a company can generate with its employees, machinery and resources in a set time.

According to the Council of Economic Experts, there is enormous variation even within the same industries. In Germany, the top companies are up to five times as productive as the weakest enterprises.

If the less productive companies caught up, economic growth could increase significantly, it said in the report. "New technologies and business models could drive peak productivity and allow new highly productive companies to develop."

But innovations need capital. It's here that the Ifo Economic Research Institute sees considerable deficiencies.

New evaluations show that German universities produce significantly fewer successful business startups than their counterparts in the United Kingdom or United States. For example, for every 1,000 students, about 14 venture capital-backed founders emerge from the vicinity of Stanford University each year. In Cambridge, the European leader, it's 3.5. In Munich, by contrast, it's only 0.5.

There continues to be an abundance of inventors and tinkerers in Germany, especially in mechanical engineering. However, the message from the industry summit in Berlin was that for renewed success, labor costs must come down. Suggestions included longer working hours and more flexibility for employers around job protection.

The intention was not to cut employees' wages and salaries. However, a new study by the German Economic Institute commissioned for the German Mechanical Engineering Industry Association showed that extending the working week by an hour alone would increase real gross domestic product by 1.5% in the coming five years.

This article was originally written in German.

#623. The secret to building Moon bases may be hiding in emergency blankets

Establishing a permanent human presence on the Moon will require more than rockets, habitats, and life support systems. Engineers must also find ways to protect astronauts and equipment from extreme temperatures that can swing from hundreds of degrees below zero to boiling hot. Reliable insulation will be essential, but keeping heat under control is only part of the problem.

Materials used in lunar construction must also survive transportation, installation, accidental impacts, and years of handling. Many of the best insulators are surprisingly delicate, making them poorly suited to the demanding conditions of a working Moon base.

Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania may have found an answer in an unexpectedly familiar material: Mylar. This lightweight plastic is used in everyday products such as food wrap and, when coated with aluminum, the reflective emergency blankets that help marathon runners retain body heat. By arranging hundreds of extremely thin Mylar sheets into carefully designed stacks, the team has created insulation that remains effective even after being bent or subjected to intense pressure.

The research, published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, introduces a material known as hybrid layered insulating film stacks (HyLIFS). Its main advantage is the ability to combine two qualities that are difficult to achieve together: excellent thermal insulation and resistance to physical damage.

"These stacks of Mylar can bend, withstand substantial compression and maintain their insulating performance," says senior author Igor Bargatin, Associate Professor in Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics (MEAM), "potentially allowing them to be packed, transported and survive rough treatment over many years of use."

If engineers can eventually manufacture the material on a large scale, it could be used to protect lunar habitats, spacesuits, and other equipment designed to function for extended periods in the vacuum of space.

"The combination of thermal and mechanical robustness is critical for long-term use on the Moon," notes first author Danielle R. Levin, a recent Penn doctoral graduate in chemistry, who also received a master's in MEAM. "This material could open a pathway to inexpensive, durable and reusable lunar insulation."

Designing insulation for the Moon involves a difficult balancing act. A material must slow the movement of heat through a vacuum while also remaining strong enough to withstand the stresses of everyday use.

Some existing materials are outstanding at preventing heat transfer but offer little protection against physical damage. Aerogels, for instance, consist mostly of empty space, which makes them extremely lightweight and effective at retaining heat. They have been used in applications ranging from industrial pipelines to NASA's Mars rovers. However, their delicate internal structure can make them vulnerable to impacts and compression.

Another widely used space technology, multilayer insulation, relies on reflective sheets separated by insulating spacers. It works particularly well at reducing heat transfer through radiation, but it is not intended to support substantial weight. Even routine contact can cause tearing or other damage.

Strengthening insulation often creates another problem: the changes that make it more durable can also allow more heat to pass through. For future lunar infrastructure, engineers need a material that can resist damage without sacrificing thermal performance.

"For lunar infrastructure, we would ideally like both," says Bargatin. "The ideal material is both resistant to damage and to the loss of heat."

How Ordinary Mylar Became Powerful Space Insulation

The Penn researchers focused on Mylar, a well-known plastic formally called biaxially oriented polyethylene terephthalate, or BoPET. Already used extensively in aerospace technology, the polymer is also found in the lightweight emergency blankets distributed after marathons. Adding a metallic coating such as aluminum allows Mylar to reflect infrared radiation, helping prevent heat from escaping.

Rather than relying on a single sheet, the researchers investigated what would happen if many thin layers were stacked together. They experimented with different film thicknesses and applied extremely thin coatings of aluminum oxide, also called alumina, to some samples to make the sheets stiffer.

Assembling the experimental stacks was surprisingly difficult. Each delicate film had to be positioned individually, requiring painstaking manual work.

"At the moment, the process is very time-consuming," says Levin. "We use two pairs of tweezers and small weights to handle and stack the delicate films. Even breathing near the stack can send the layers flying."

Despite the simplicity of the basic idea, testing revealed an impressive combination of properties. In a vacuum, the best stacks achieved thermal conductivity comparable to other advanced vacuum insulation materials while retaining their flexibility.

The researchers also tested the material under compression similar to what insulation could experience inside a lunar habitat, where the interior air pressure would push against walls exposed to the vacuum outside.

Additional mechanical testing showed that stacks coated with alumina could tolerate the greatest compressive stresses available with the laboratory equipment while maintaining their insulating performance. The results demonstrated that improving durability did not necessarily require giving up thermal protection.

Crushing Pressure Reveals Unexpected Durability

One of the most striking findings came when the team subjected the material to repeated compression. Even the researchers were surprised by how well the thin plastic layers held up.

The samples were compressed to approximately 20 megapascals, a pressure comparable to concentrating 200 pounds of force onto an area the size of a fingertip. Instead of testing the material only once, the researchers repeated the process 10 times.

"We were concerned about the material failing under such high compressive stress," recalls Levin. "But the stacks didn't survive just one high stress cycle -- they survived 10 in a row."

This resistance to damage could be especially valuable for lunar exploration. Every piece of equipment needed on the Moon must first endure the challenges of being packed, launched, transported, and installed. Insulation that can bend, withstand pressure, and potentially be reused would offer significant practical advantages.

Durability would remain important after construction is complete. Astronauts living and working inside a lunar habitat could accidentally strike or compress insulation during maintenance or ordinary activities.

"You could use these stacks to insulate a lunar habitation, but astronauts will inevitably have little accidents where they bump into them," notes Bargatin. "When we're talking about long-term habitation on the moon, it's really important to have tough materials that can last long enough."

Tiny Particles Reveal a Hidden Secret of Heat Transfer

Beyond demonstrating the material's durability, the experiments uncovered an important clue about how heat travels through layers of Mylar.

The discovery involved microscopic particles already present in commercially manufactured plastic films. Extremely thin sheets naturally tend to stick to one another and to nearby surfaces, which complicates manufacturing and handling. To prevent this, producers add tiny "antiblocking" particles that extend slightly above the plastic surface and keep neighboring sheets from clinging together.

Although manufacturers have long understood why these particles are useful, their influence on heat transfer in stacked Mylar films had received relatively little attention.

Traditional multilayer space insulation is primarily designed to control heat transferred by radiation. As a result, researchers have had less reason to investigate how small points of physical contact between films might affect heat conduction.

The Penn team examined this possibility by constructing mathematical models of heat transfer between individual layers and comparing the predictions with laboratory measurements.

The findings indicate that, in a vacuum, much of the heat moving from one Mylar sheet to the next passes through the tiny contact points created by the antiblocking particles.

That result could have important implications for future insulation design. Instead of accepting the particles as an incidental feature of commercial plastic, engineers might deliberately control their size, abundance, and placement to reduce unwanted heat transfer.

Why Thinner Plastic Does Not Always Insulate Better

The role of these microscopic particles also helped explain another unexpected result.

At first, the researchers assumed that thinner Mylar sheets would produce better insulation. Using thinner films would allow more layers to occupy the same amount of space, increasing the number of boundaries that heat must cross.

However, the experiments did not fully support that expectation. When coated with alumina, the thinnest films the team successfully characterized provided thermal performance similar to films of medium thickness.

The researchers suspect that the antiblocking particles help explain why. In thinner sheets, the particles can produce more contact between adjacent layers, creating additional routes for heat to move through the material. Those extra contact points can offset the expected advantages of adding more layers.

The finding suggests that making films thinner is not automatically the best approach. Engineers must also consider how the sheets bend and deform under pressure, along with the number and arrangement of microscopic contact points.

"As you compress the layers, the contact landscape changes," says Levin. "It's not just a matter of minimizing the film thickness or the number of particles; we must also account for how the contacts change and the films deform as pressure increases."

Ultimately, the ability of these stacks to limit heat transfer depends on several interacting factors, including the thickness and stiffness of the plastic and the distribution of particles within it.

From Tiny Laboratory Samples to Future Moon Bases

Although the early results are encouraging, the new insulation is still far from being ready for lunar construction.

The experimental HyLIFS samples currently measure only about one square centimeter, and producing them requires hours of careful cutting and manual stacking. That painstaking process would be impractical for manufacturing the large sheets needed to insulate an entire habitat.

To make the material useful on a larger scale, the researchers will need a more efficient production method. One possibility involves continuously applying coatings to large rolls of Mylar, using manufacturing techniques that could eventually produce sheets measured in meters rather than centimeters.

Such an approach might also allow engineers to adjust the thickness of the plastic, the protective coatings, and the distribution of antiblocking particles before assembling the material into larger stacks.

Important questions remain. The researchers still need to determine whether large versions of the material will retain the same insulating properties and mechanical strength seen in the laboratory. Further testing must also establish how well the stacks tolerate repeated bending, accidental impacts, scratches, and other wear associated with real-world use.

If those challenges can be overcome, the technology could provide lightweight, flexible, durable insulation for lunar habitats, rovers, electronic equipment, and other systems operating in space.

For Levin, the results also offer a broader lesson about materials engineering. Even familiar products can reveal unexpected capabilities when researchers examine how their structures behave under different conditions.

"The simplest configuration ended up being the best one," she says.

The research was carried out at the University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science (Penn Engineering). Additional co-authors include Matthew F. Campbell, Gulzhan Aldan, and Orevaoghene H. Omodior.

Funding was provided by the National Science Foundation Division of Chemical, Bioengineering, Environmental and Transport Systems (grant number 1845933) and Penn Engineering.

"A space-based capability such as this could cause rapid and sudden loss or degradation of thousands of satellites operated by countries and companies around the world."

Last month, the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) released a chilling and info-packed report judging the scope and breadth of threats posed by the nation's adversaries in space.

The new report focuses on China, Russia and the emerging space powers of Iran and North Korea. It looks at what's happening in Earth orbit and beyond, including cislunar space, the region between our planet and the moon.

The report — the 2026 edition of "Challenges to Security in Space" — is the third iteration of the DIA's unclassified intelligence assessment on space-related challenges and threats to U.S. national security, as well as the extent to which space is treated internationally as a warfighting domain.

Information within the report, which you can read here, is current as of July 2026. DIA's mission is to provide intelligence on foreign militaries to help prevent wars, and win the ones that are fought.

The report's up-front finding is that China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea are developing, testing, deploying and using space capabilities "in a way that threatens the security of all space systems and their associated space benefits."

Indeed, China and Russia are developing "a formidable spectrum" of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations.

The DIA report also notes that "the production of cheaper, smaller, and simpler satellites, which are faster to develop and deploy, along with the expansion of commercially available launch services, are driving the rapid integration of commercial space alternatives to support national security."

While space commercialization is making previously government-centered space services widely available to interested parties, the DIA report adds, that availability also includes state and non-state actors with malign interests.

A major item dealt with by the DIA is "counterspace" — and it's not the kind that you'll find in your kitchen.

Counterspace operations can be either offensive or defensive. They can be used on purpose to reversibly or irreversibly deny, disrupt, degrade, damage or destroy a space object or component of a space system.

Here are the key elements of counterspace, as identified within the DIA report:

The DIA report underscores that Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon.

Russia is doing so despite its obligation to comply with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. That U.N. agreement prohibits the placement of any objects carrying nuclear weapons, or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction, into orbit around Earth.

"A space-based capability such as this could cause rapid and sudden loss or degradation of thousands of satellites operated by countries and companies around the world," the DIA report states, "as well as to the vital communications, navigation, scientific, meteorological, commercial and national security services they provide."

A nuclear detonation in space could be tailored to impact satellites in most orbits, the DIA report warns, from low Earth orbit for commercial and reconnaissance satellites, geosynchronous orbit for critical communications, and medium Earth orbit for navigation and timing satellites.

The newly issued DIA report also observes that exploring cislunar space is of increasing interest to spacefaring nations for potential scientific and economic opportunities. However, nations such as China "may be exploring military applications from cislunar space," the report notes.

China has stated its goal of developing a cislunar space economy by 2045.

"China is also the first country to attempt sustained operations on the far side of the moon, with numerous projects slated to support that effort through the next decade. China portrays its interest in cislunar space as peaceful, but PRC [People's Republic of China] officials have also discussed pursuing military capabilities in cislunar space," the report states.

Placing a keen eye on the DIA report is Peter Garretson, a senior fellow in defense studies at the American Foreign Policy Council and a strategy consultant who focuses on space and defense.

According to Garretson, the most significant positive change from earlier DIA appraisals is the explicit assessment that Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon. He told Space.com that the DIA's expanded treatment of the threat of a nuclear weapon on orbit reflects concerns in the Congress and the Trump White House.

However, Garretson also flagged what he said is a consequential omission in the report: the disappearance of the prior treatment (in the 2022 version of the report) of research competition, surveillance beyond geosynchronous Earth orbit and the potential military use of deep space for staging reserve forces.

In Garretson's view, the DIA needs to help put the puzzle pieces together for Congress and the attentive public about what exactly China is doing, and how it fits together in the nation's strategy to achieve comprehensive space dominance.

According to Garretson, "everything they are doing, from launch cadence, reusable launch, commercial space investment, investments in power, propulsion, repair, manufacturing, to commercial assets working together" supports both an economic expansion toward new resources and what China hopes will be overwhelming military power and strategic depth.

Garretson senses the moves by China to develop extractive and in-space industries "is truly the strategic threat that could crush American space power. Now is the time to be making the investments to ensure we have a 'freedom's forge' and 'arsenal of democracy' in space that can protect the open space commerce that is the nation's strategy."

As for the DIA's outlook for the future: The agency concluded that space almost certainly will remain an increasingly competitive and crowded environment as space capabilities improve and other countries seize opportunities in the final frontier.

"The increase of Chinese, Russian, Iranian and North Korean counterspace capabilities, rapid growth in the number of space objects, and the proliferation of requirements for space-enabled services," the DIA report states, "will all complicate operations in space in the coming decade."

#621. A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret

Scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal. Known as a heavy fermion state, this phenomenon causes electrons to behave as though they have much greater mass than normal. These states are associated with extraordinary quantum effects, including unconventional superconductivity, and the discovery could provide a new way to develop materials with unusual electronic properties.

To investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal. They then used powerful synchrotron light to study the electrons and their interactions at the boundary between the two materials. The results showed that electrons confined to the thin atomic layer could interact with freely moving electrons in the copper beneath it, producing the unusual heavy fermion behavior.

The experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics. One existed primarily within the two-dimensional atomic layer, while the other reached beyond that layer and into the three-dimensional copper crystal below.

The second state was particularly important because it provided the first direct evidence of heavy fermion behavior generated by interactions across such an interface. Researchers traced the effect to the mixing, or hybridization, of localized ytterbium 4f electrons in the atomic layer with mobile conduction electrons inside the copper substrate. This interaction demonstrated how combining materials with different electronic characteristics can produce quantum behavior that neither material would necessarily exhibit on its own.

"This achievement was made possible by our continued efforts to create high-quality materials and measure their electronic states as precisely as possible," says senior author Professor Shin-ichi Kimura. "Our next goal is to engineer and control such heavy-electron states, opening the way to previously unexplored quantum states, including unconventional superconductivity."

A New Approach to Designing Quantum Materials

The discovery suggests that the boundaries between materials could become powerful tools for creating and controlling exotic quantum states. Rather than relying only on the properties of individual substances, scientists may be able to develop entirely new electronic behaviors by carefully selecting and combining ultrathin atomic layers with suitable underlying materials.

Future research could focus on adjusting the structures of these interfaces, controlling the electronic orbitals involved, and manipulating moiré patterns that arise when atomic arrangements overlap. Such approaches may allow researchers to produce and fine-tune quantum phenomena in materials with extremely small dimensions, including effects that cannot be achieved in conventional materials. Ultimately, this could open new possibilities for engineering advanced quantum materials and investigating unconventional superconductivity.
